sections.title: Start here
intro: This guide explains every word, sign and idea you meet in the app, starting from nothing. You don't need to have learned another language before. Each entry starts with a one-line answer, then explains more slowly, with real examples from the Bible that you can hear and open in the Reader.
Tap any underlined word to read its own entry. Tap Greek or Hebrew to hear it.

sections.title: Grammar words everyone needs
intro: Grammar has its own words, and they can make a simple idea sound hard. This section explains the ones you will meet, using English first. Every one of them is something you already use without thinking when you speak English.
Read these in order if grammar is new to you. Each takes a minute or two.

sections.title: Greek letters, marks and punctuation
intro: Printed Greek has small marks above and beside its letters, and a few punctuation signs of its own. Most were added long after the New Testament was written, to help readers. This section explains each one. The Letters tab covers the alphabet itself, letter by letter, with sounds.

sections.title: Greek nouns, “the” and pronouns
intro: Greek nouns, adjectives, pronouns and the word “the” change their endings to show what job they do in the sentence. This section explains those endings, called cases, the three families of nouns, and the different kinds of pronoun.

sections.title: Greek verbs
intro: A Greek verb packs a lot into one word: what happens, who does it, how the action is viewed, whether it is a statement, a wish or a command, and whether the subject does it or has it done to them. This section takes those pieces one at a time.

sections.title: Hebrew letters, vowels and signs
intro: Hebrew is written from right to left, with consonant letters and small marks for the vowels and accents. A page of the Hebrew Bible can look crowded, but each mark has one job. This section explains them one by one. The Letters tab shows every letter and vowel with its sound.

sections.title: Hebrew words: roots, nouns and the little words
intro: Hebrew builds its words on a root of consonants and joins many small words to the front or back of the main word. One Hebrew word can be a whole English phrase: וּבְבֵיתוֹ, “and in his house”. This section explains how to take such a word apart.

sections.title: Hebrew verbs
intro: A Hebrew verb is built from three things: a root that gives the basic meaning, a stem pattern that gives the kind of action (simple, intensive, causative, passive), and a form with prefixes or endings that shows who does it and how the action is viewed. This section explains each, in the order a grammar label lists them.

sections.title: Biblical Aramaic
intro: A few chapters of the Old Testament are in Aramaic, Hebrew's close relative. Its letters, vowels and much of its vocabulary are the same, but its verb stems have different names and its word for “the” is an ending. This section explains the labels you will meet there.

sections.title: Using the app
intro: The last section explains the app itself: each tab and screen, what a tapped word shows, the short forms used under words, how Review decides what to show you, and how listening, offline use, backups and updates work.

entries.title: Using this guide
entries.short: Search for a word, browse by section, or tap “What do these words mean?” under any grammar in the app.

body.p: There are three ways in. You can type a word in the search box at the top of the Guide tab: an English word such as “aorist”, an abbreviation such as “impf.” or “3ms”, or a grammar code such as V-2AAI-3S. You can browse the sections, which go from the simplest ideas to the hardest. Or you can start from the Bible: when you tap a word in the Reader, on Today or in a lesson, its grammar has a link, “What do these words mean?”, which explains each part.
Entries link to each other. If an explanation uses a word you don't know yet, that word is underlined: tap it, read the short answer, and come back with the back button.
Most entries end with examples from the Bible. The word the entry is about is highlighted. Tap Listen to hear it, or “Open in the Reader” to see it in its chapter.

If you are just starting, read the section [[grammar|Grammar words everyone needs]] first. It explains words such as [[noun]], [[verb]] and [[subject]] using English, before any Greek or Hebrew. Then read about the letters and marks of each language ([[greek-alphabet|Greek]], [[hebrew-alphabet|Hebrew]]) before their grammar.

entries.title: Koine Greek
entries.short: The everyday Greek spoken around the eastern Mediterranean in the time of Jesus, and the language of the New Testament.

body.p: Greek has been written for nearly three thousand years. The kind used in the New Testament is called Koine, a Greek word meaning “common” or “shared”. After the conquests of Alexander the Great, Greek became the shared language of trade, government and travel from Egypt to Mesopotamia and beyond. Many people spoke it as a second language.

The writers of the New Testament wrote in this common Greek, not in the polished Greek of the older classical writers. That is good news for a learner: its sentences are usually direct, and a small number of words make up most of the text.

Koine is written with the same alphabet as Greek today, but it is not the same as Modern Greek. Many words are spelt the same, while their sounds, some endings and many meanings have changed. Greek Bibles also add [[accents]] and [[breathing|breathing marks]] that the first writers didn't use.
The Old Testament was also translated into Koine before the time of Jesus: see [[septuagint]].

entries.title: Biblical Hebrew
match: Hebrew=Hebrew, not Aramaic
entries.short: The language in which almost all of the Old Testament was written.

body.p: Hebrew belongs to the same family of languages as Aramaic and Arabic. It was spoken in ancient Israel, and the books of the Old Testament were written in it over many centuries. A few chapters are in Aramaic instead: see [[aramaic-language]].

Hebrew is written from right to left. Its alphabet has only consonants: the vowels were added later as small dots and dashes around the letters ([[vowel-points]]). Most words are built on a [[root]] of three consonants, and a great deal of the meaning comes from the vowels and the small additions placed around that root.

Modern Hebrew, spoken in Israel today, grew out of Biblical Hebrew. The letters and many words are the same, but the grammar and vocabulary have changed. The app's pronunciation is based on how Hebrew is said today, the way most colleges teach it: see [[hebrew-pronunciation]].

entries.title: Biblical Aramaic
match: Aramaic=Aramaic, not Hebrew
entries.short: A sister language of Hebrew, used in a few chapters of Daniel and Ezra and in some words of Jesus.

body.p: Aramaic was the shared language of the Persian Empire, and many Jews spoke it after the exile. It uses the same letters and vowel signs as Hebrew, and many words are similar, so the Reader shows it in the same way, with a small “Aram.” beside the verse.

In the Old Testament, Aramaic is used in [DAN 2:4|Daniel 2:4] to the end of chapter seven, in Ezra 4:8–6:18 and Ezra 7:12–26, in one verse of Jeremiah ([JER 10:11]) and in two words of Genesis ([GEN 31:47]).

The New Testament is in Greek, but it keeps a few Aramaic words just as Jesus said them, written in Greek letters: Ταλιθα κουμ in [MRK 5:41], and Αββα, “Father”, in [MRK 14:36]. The [[grammar-labels]] call these “transcribed from Aramaic”. See [[aramaic-stems]] for how Aramaic verbs are labelled.

entries.title: The Septuagint
entries.short: The Greek translation of the Old Testament, made by Jewish translators in the centuries before Jesus.

body.p: The Septuagint was translated from Hebrew into [[koine-greek]], beginning in Alexandria in Egypt with the five books of Moses. Its name is Latin for “seventy”. An old story says seventy-two translators made it, and the number was rounded. LXX is seventy in Roman numerals.

It matters for two reasons. The New Testament writers often quote it, so its wording is behind many New Testament quotations. And it shows how Jews of that time understood Hebrew words in Greek, which helps with the meaning of both languages.

The Septuagint doesn't always match the Hebrew text verse for verse: some books are arranged differently, some are longer or shorter, and it includes books that are not in the Hebrew Bible. The app uses the edition by H. B. Swete, printed in Cambridge. In the Reader you can show it under the Hebrew, or read it on its own from the book list. Its words are not tagged with grammar, so a tapped word is looked up by its spelling: see [[septuagint-lookup]].

entries.title: The Greek New Testament in the app
entries.short: The app's New Testament is the SBL Greek New Testament, an edition made by comparing the manuscripts.

body.p: No original letter of Paul or first copy of a Gospel survives. What we have are thousands of handwritten copies (manuscripts) made over many centuries, and they differ in small ways. Scholars compare them to work out the most likely original wording: see [[manuscripts]].

The app uses the SBL Greek New Testament, edited by Michael Holmes and published by the Society of Biblical Literature. It is free to share, which is why the app can use it. Its wording is very close to the other editions used in colleges.
Every word is tagged with its [[dictionary-form]], its meaning in that verse and its grammar, using data from [[stepbible]]. The [[grammar-labels]] are explained in their own entry.

entries.title: The Hebrew Bible in the app
entries.short: The app's Old Testament is the Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete handwritten copy of the Hebrew Bible.

body.p: The Leningrad Codex was copied around the year 1008 and is now kept in St Petersburg (once called Leningrad). It is a careful copy of the text handed down by the [[masoretes]], the scribes who added the vowels and [[cantillation|accent marks]].

Because it is complete and carefully made, the standard scholarly editions of the Hebrew Bible are based on it. The app uses [[stepbible|STEPBible]]'s edition, in which every word is split into its parts and tagged with its meaning and grammar.

Sometimes a word is written one way but read another way, and the Masoretes noted both: see [[ketiv-qere]]. A few words missing from the Hebrew manuscripts are supplied from other ancient sources: see [[supplied-words]].

entries.title: The Masoretes
entries.short: The Jewish scribes who, over several centuries, added vowels, accents and notes to the Hebrew text so it would be read exactly as handed down.

body.p: For most of its history the Hebrew Bible was written with consonants only. Readers knew the vowels from memory and from hearing the text read aloud. Between about the sixth and tenth centuries, scholars in Tiberias, by the Sea of Galilee, invented a system of marks to record the reading they had received, without changing a single letter.

They added three kinds of marks: [[vowel-points]], which show the vowels; [[cantillation|accent]] marks, which show the stress, the pauses and how the verse was chanted; and notes in the margins counting words and letters and recording places where a word is read differently from how it is written ([[ketiv-qere]]).

entries.title: Manuscripts and different readings
entries.short: Handwritten copies of the Bible differ in small ways; scholars compare them to find the most likely original wording.

body.p: Before printing, every copy of a book was written out by hand. Copyists sometimes made slips, like a word written twice or a line skipped, and sometimes tidied the wording. So the thousands of surviving manuscripts differ here and there. Most differences are tiny, such as spelling or word order, and very few change the meaning of a sentence.

Printed Greek and Hebrew Bibles choose one reading for the main text and often list other readings at the foot of the page (the apparatus). The app shows the main text only. Where a whole passage is doubtful, as in [MRK 16:9] or [JHN 7:53], the Greek text puts it in [[double-brackets]] and the Reader explains why.

entries.title: STEPBible
entries.short: A free Bible-study website made by researchers at Tyndale House, Cambridge. Its tagging of every Greek and Hebrew word is what the app's word details are built on.

body.p: STEPBible's team tagged every word of the Greek New Testament and the Hebrew Bible with its [[dictionary-form]], its meaning in that verse and its grammar, and published the work for anyone to use. The app uses that work: when this guide says “STEPBible's labels”, it means the wording of those tags.
Their work is careful, but a project this size has slips. Where the app has found one, such as a word tagged with a form it can't have, it corrects it and notes the change in the app's documentation.

entries.title: The English translations
entries.short: The Reader shows the Berean Standard Bible under each verse, and the ESV too if you add your own free key.

body.p: The Berean Standard Bible (BSB) is a modern translation that is free for anyone to use, so the app can include all of it. It is shown under each verse and in the word details.

The English Standard Version (ESV) belongs to its publisher, Crossway. They give a free access code (they call it a “key”) to anyone for personal use: you request one on Crossway's ESV website, then enter it in Settings, and the ESV shows in the Reader alongside the BSB. Only a small part is ever saved on your phone, as the publisher asks.

A translation turns whole sentences into natural English, so the English words don't line up one for one with the Greek or Hebrew. The meaning shown under each original word is closer to the word itself: see [[gloss]].

entries.title: Chapters and verse numbers
entries.short: Chapters and verses were added long after the Bible was written, and editions sometimes number them differently.

body.p: The writers didn't divide their books into chapters and verses. Chapters were added in the Middle Ages, and verse numbers later still, for finding places. Different traditions didn't always divide the text in the same place.

The app uses English numbering everywhere so the original and the translation line up. Where Hebrew Bibles number a verse differently, the Reader shows a small “Heb” number under it. This happens most in the Psalms, where Hebrew Bibles often count a psalm's title as a verse: see [[psalm-titles]].

The Greek New Testament and the English also differ in a few places. Some verses printed in older English Bibles are not in the best manuscripts, so they are missing from both the Greek and the BSB, and the numbering simply skips them: after [MAT 17:20|Matthew 17:20] comes verse twenty-two. The Reader puts a note wherever the two don't match.

entries.title: Strong's numbers
entries.short: A number for each Hebrew and Greek dictionary word, so you can look a word up without knowing the language.

body.p: James Strong published a huge index of the English Bible in 1890, and gave each Hebrew and Greek dictionary word a number. Hebrew words have numbers starting H, Greek words numbers starting G: H430 is אֱלֹהִים, God, and G3056 is λόγος, word. Many books and websites still use them.

The app uses STEPBible's improved version. Where one of Strong's numbers covers two different words, or different meanings of one word, STEPBible adds a letter to tell them apart. You can type a Strong's number into the [[words-tab|Words tab]] to find its entry.

entries.title: Dictionary form
entries.short: The form of a word you look up in a dictionary, such as “run” for “ran” and “running”.

body.p: Words change their shape in a sentence. In English, “ran”, “runs” and “running” are all forms of “run”. A dictionary lists only “run”. That basic form is called the dictionary form (or lemma).

Greek and Hebrew change shape much more than English. One Greek verb can appear in more than a hundred different forms. So in the app, every word in the Bible shows both what it is in that verse and its dictionary form. Greek verbs are listed by their “I” form: πιστεύω, “I believe”. Greek nouns are listed in the [[nominative]] singular: λόγος. Hebrew verbs are listed by their simplest “he did” form: בָּרָא, “he created”. Grammar books call this the [[qal]] [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]].
When you tap a word, you see the form in the verse first, then “Dictionary form”. In the [[words-tab|Words tab]] you can search for either.

entries.title: Gloss and meaning
entries.short: A gloss is a short meaning for a word: one or two English words, not a full definition.

body.p: When you tap a word, the app shows three kinds of meaning. “In this verse” is the English for this word in this place, from STEPBible's word-by-word translation. “Dictionary meaning” is the usual meaning of the [[dictionary-form]]. The full entry in the [[words-tab|Words tab]] gives a longer definition from an older dictionary.
These short meanings are called glosses.

Words in square brackets, such as [the], are added in English to make sense but have no word of their own in Greek or Hebrew. Words in angle brackets, such as <the>, are in the original but are not translated, because English doesn't need them.

entries.title: Transliteration
entries.short: Writing a Greek or Hebrew word in our alphabet, letter by letter, so you can see what it is made of.

body.p: A transliteration replaces each Greek or Hebrew letter with a letter or two of ours: λόγος becomes logos. It is a help for reading, not an exact guide to sound. The app's transliterations come from STEPBible. In them, η and ω, which were once said longer than ε and ο, carry a line (ē, ō), and Hebrew syllables are divided with dots, with the [[stress|stressed]] syllable starting with a capital. In the Reader's display options this line is called **Pronunciation**.
For how to say a word, follow the simpler [[respelling|respelling]] on cards and in lessons, such as LO-gos.

entries.title: Saying a word: the respelling
entries.short: The app writes how a word sounds in plain English letters, with the stressed syllable in capitals: LO-gos.

body.p: Next to many words you will see a respelling such as LO-gos or e-lo-HIM. The hyphens split the word into syllables, and the syllable in capitals is the one to stress, the way we stress the first syllable of “TA-ble”.

For Greek the respelling follows the [[erasmian|Erasmian]] pronunciation. For Hebrew it follows the [[hebrew-pronunciation|pronunciation taught in most colleges]]. A few combinations need a word of explanation: kh is the sound at the end of Scottish “loch”; ch in Hebrew respellings is the same throat sound (never as in “church”); i in Hebrew respellings is said as in “machine”; and ü in Greek is said like German ü or French “tu”: round your lips for “oo” and say “ee”.

entries.title: Erasmian pronunciation
entries.short: The way most colleges pronounce New Testament Greek, keeping almost every letter's sound distinct.

body.p: Nobody can hear first-century Greek, so learners need an agreed way of saying it. The Erasmian pronunciation is named after the scholar Erasmus, who wrote about how ancient Greek may have sounded. It gives nearly every letter and pair of letters its own sound; only a few share one (η and ει are both “ay”). The [[greek-alphabet|Greek alphabet]] and the [[letters-tab|Letters tab]] give each letter's sound.

Its great advantage is spelling: if you hear a word, you can usually tell how it is written. It is not how Greek sounded in the time of Jesus, and it is not how Greek sounds today. The app uses it by default, and the lessons write pronunciations this way. You can switch to [[restored-koine]] in Settings.

entries.title: Restored Koine pronunciation
entries.short: An attempt to say New Testament Greek as it was said in the first century, closer to Modern Greek.

body.p: Scholars, especially Randall Buth, have worked out from spelling mistakes in ancient papyri (letters and documents written on papyrus, a kind of paper), poetry and later Greek how Koine probably sounded in the first century. By then several vowels and pairs had merged: ει and ι were both “ee”, αι sounded like the e in “get”, and υ and οι both sounded like French “u”. β was already v, and δ was like the “th” in “this”.

Choose it in Settings if you want to hear the Greek closer to how the apostles spoke. The respellings in the app stay [[erasmian|Erasmian]], so the letters stay clear. Because the app's Greek voice is a modern one, a few first-century sounds can only be imitated.

entries.title: Hebrew pronunciation in the app
entries.short: The app says Hebrew the way most colleges teach it: based on Israeli Hebrew, with every written vowel said.

body.p: There is no single way of saying [[biblical-hebrew]]. The app follows the pronunciation taught in most colleges, which is based on how Hebrew is spoken in Israel today. For example, ח is a throat sound like the end of Scottish “loch”, and the letters א and ע are silent.

Two rules keep it closer to the written text than everyday Israeli speech: a [[shewa]] at the start of a syllable is said as a quick e (בְּרִית is be-RIT, not brit), and the [[qamets-hatuf]] is said o. God's name is read Adonai, as Jewish readers say it: see [[divine-name]].
The [[masoretes]] who wrote the vowels heard more differences than we make today. The [[letters-tab|Letters tab]] explains how it sounded then.

entries.title: Grammar labels
entries.short: Each word in the Bible has a label naming its grammar, such as “Verb aorist active indicative 3rd singular”. This guide explains every word in them.

body.p: [[stepbible|STEPBible]] tags every word of the Greek and Hebrew with a short code, such as V-AAI-3S for a Greek verb or HVqp3ms for a Hebrew verb. The app turns each code into words: “Verb aorist active indicative 3rd singular”. Under each word in the Reader there is a shorter version with abbreviations, such as “verb aor. act. ind. 3rd sg.”: see [[abbreviations]].

A label lists the facts a reader needs in order to understand the word: what kind of word it is ([[word-classes|its part of speech]]), and then, for a verb, its [[tense]] or form, [[voice]], [[mood]] and [[person]], and for a noun its [[case]], [[number]] and [[gender]].

Below most labels the app adds STEPBible's plain description and a sample English phrase, such as “he taught”. These samples use made-up example words to show the shape of the meaning, not the meaning of this word.
Tap “What do these words mean?” under any grammar in the app to see each part explained.

entries.title: How common a word is
entries.short: The number of times a dictionary word appears in the New Testament or Old Testament text the app uses.

body.p: Under each word's details, and in the [[words-tab|Words tab]], the app counts how often its [[dictionary-form]] appears. A small number of words make up most of the text, so learning the common words first pays off quickly. καί, “and”, appears {{kai}} times in the New Testament.
The Review tab's word lists are built from these counts, most common first.

entries.title: What grammar is
entries.short: Grammar is the set of patterns a language uses to show how words fit together and who does what to whom.

body.p: In “the dog bit the man”, English shows who did the biting by the order of the words: swap them and the meaning changes. Greek and Hebrew show much of this with changes to the words themselves, mostly with [[inflection|endings]], prefixes and changes of vowel. That is why a Greek or Hebrew word comes with a label naming its grammar.

You don't need to memorise every label. Most of the time you only need to know three things about a word: what kind of word it is (its [[word-classes|part of speech]]), what job it is doing in the sentence, and, for a [[verb]], who is doing it. The entries in this section explain the words used to describe those things.

entries.title: Parts of speech
entries.short: The kinds of word a language has: naming words, doing words, describing words and so on.

body.p: Every word belongs to a kind, called its part of speech. The first word of every grammar label in the app tells you which kind it is. The main kinds are:

ul: a [[noun]] names a person, place or thing: “shepherd”, “Jerusalem”, “love”;
a [[pronoun]] stands in for a noun: “he”, “them”, “who”;
a [[verb]] says what happens or what someone does: “runs”, “was”, “will save”;
an [[adjective]] describes a noun: “good shepherd”;
an [[adverb]] describes how, when or where: “quickly”, “then”, “there”;
an [[article|article]] is the word “the” (or “a”);
a [[preposition]] shows how one thing relates to another: “in”, “from”, “with”;
a [[conjunction]] joins words or sentences: “and”, “but”, “because”;
a [[particle]] is a small word that adds a shade of meaning, such as “not”;
an [[interjection]] is an exclamation: “Oh!”, “Look!”.

entries.title: Noun
match: noun
entries.short: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea: “shepherd”, “city”, “love”.

body.p: Nouns are naming words. Anything you can put “the” in front of is probably a noun: the shepherd, the city, the word, the love of God. Names of particular people and places, such as Peter or Galilee, are nouns too: see [[proper-noun]].

In English a noun changes little: “word” becomes “words” for more than one. In Greek a noun also changes its ending to show its job in the sentence (its [[case]]). In Hebrew a noun can take a prefix such as “and”, “the” or “in”, and an ending such as “my” or “their”, all written as one word.
Every Greek and Hebrew noun also has a [[gender]], and is either one or more than one (its [[number]]).

entries.title: Names: proper nouns
match: proper noun
name=a name
of a type=a describing word used as a name or title, such as the Beautiful Gate
name of a person=the name of a particular person
name of a place=the name of a particular place
title=a title or a name used like one
people group=a word for a people, such as Galileans
individual=the name of a particular person
location=the name of a particular place
entries.short: The name of a particular person, place or thing, such as Jesus, Moses or Jerusalem.

body.p: A proper noun is a name. In English we give names a capital letter: Peter, Galilee, Passover. Greek Bibles also start names with a capital letter. Hebrew has no capital letters, so the grammar label tells you instead.

STEPBible's labels sort names into kinds, and the app shows them in brackets: the name of a person, the name of a place, a title (such as “Christ” or a month's name), or a people group (such as “Galilean”, see [[gentilic]]).
Many names in the New Testament are Hebrew or Aramaic names written in Greek letters, and some of these never change their ending: see [[indeclinable]] and [[transcribed]].

entries.title: Pronoun
match: pronoun
personal pronoun
personal
entries.short: A word that stands in for a noun: “he”, “she”, “it”, “we”, “they”, “who”, “this”.

body.p: Instead of saying “Peter took Peter's boat”, we say “Peter took *his* boat”. Words like “I”, “you”, “he”, “his”, “them” and “who” are pronouns.

Greek has separate pronoun words, as English does, and they change their ending like nouns: see [[personal-pronoun]]. Hebrew has separate pronoun words for “I”, “you”, “he” and so on, but more often it adds a short ending to a word instead: “his word” is one word, דְּבָרוֹ. See [[pronoun-suffix]].

Pronouns come in several kinds, each with its own entry: personal (“he”), [[possessive]] (“my”), [[reflexive]] (“himself”), [[reciprocal]] (“one another”), [[demonstrative]] (“this”, “that”), [[relative]] (“who”, “which”), [[interrogative]] (“who?”) and [[indefinite]] (“someone”).

entries.title: Verb
match: verb
entries.short: A word for what happens or what someone does or is: “runs”, “said”, “will save”, “is”.

body.p: Verbs are the doing and being words. In “Jesus wept”, the verb is “wept”. Every complete sentence has one, though Hebrew and Greek can leave out “is” where English needs it: see [[verbless-clause]].

English shows the time of an action mostly with helper words: “I *will* go”, “I *was* going”. Greek and Hebrew show most of this, and who is doing it, inside the verb itself, with endings, prefixes and changes of vowel. One Greek or Hebrew verb can therefore be a whole English sentence: ἐδάκρυσεν, “he wept”.

A verb's grammar label describes it with several words: see [[tense]], [[aspect]], [[voice]], [[mood]], [[person]] and [[number]]. How verbs are built is explained in [[greek-verb]] and [[hebrew-verb]].

entries.title: Adjective
match: adjective
entries.short: A word that describes a noun: “good”, “holy”, “first”.

body.p: In “the good shepherd”, “good” is an adjective: it tells you what the shepherd is like. In English an adjective never changes. In Greek and Hebrew it changes to match the noun it describes, in [[gender]] and [[number]] (and in Greek in [[case]] too). This matching is called [[agreement]].
In both languages an adjective can also be used on its own as a noun, the way English says “the poor” or “the holy”: ὁ ἅγιος, “the holy one”.

entries.title: Adverb
match: adverb
adverb or adverb and particle combined=an adverb with a small word such as “not” built into it
combined=two words joined into one
entries.short: A word that says how, when, where or how much: “quickly”, “now”, “there”, “very”.

body.p: An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence, rather than a noun. In “he went out immediately”, “immediately” is an adverb. Many Greek adverbs end in -ως, as many English ones end in “-ly”: οὕτως, “in this way”. Adverbs don't change their form.

entries.title: The article, “the”
match: definite article
article
entries.short: The word “the”. Greek and Hebrew have “the” but no word for “a”.

body.p: English has two articles: “the” (the definite article) and “a” or “an” (the indefinite article). Greek and Hebrew have only “the”. Where there is no “the”, [[translations|English translations]] often add “a”: λόγος can be “a word”.

The two languages use “the” differently from English, and from each other. In Greek it is a separate word that changes its ending to match its noun, and it is used far more than English uses “the”, even before names: see [[greek-article]]. In Hebrew it is a prefix, הַ, joined to the front of the word: see [[hebrew-article]].

entries.title: Preposition
match: preposition
entries.short: A small word that shows how one thing relates to another: “in”, “from”, “with”, “to”, “under”.

body.p: In “the Word was with God”, “with” is a preposition: it shows how the Word relates to God. A preposition goes before a noun or pronoun.

In Greek a preposition is a separate word, and the noun after it takes a particular [[case]]. Some Greek prepositions change their meaning with the case: μετά with one case means “with”, with another “after”. In Hebrew three common prepositions are one letter long and are joined to the front of the next word: see [[hebrew-prepositions]].

entries.title: Conjunction
match: conjunction
entries.short: A word that joins words or sentences together: “and”, “but”, “for”, “because”, “if”.

body.p: Conjunctions are the joints of a sentence. καί, “and”, is the commonest word in the New Testament after “the”. Hebrew joins almost every sentence of a story with “and”, written as a one-letter prefix: see [[conjunction-vav|the entry on וְ]].
[[translations|English translations]] often leave these “and”s out or turn them into “then”, “so” or “but”, because English doesn't like starting every sentence with “and”.

entries.title: Particle
match: particle
disjunctive=offering a choice, such as “or”
entries.short: A small word that doesn't change its form and adds a shade of meaning: “not”, “indeed”, “then”.

body.p: Particle is a catch-all name for small words that are not nouns, verbs or adjectives and never change their form. Greek has many: some make a sentence negative (οὐ, “not”), some ask a question, and some show how a sentence connects to the one before, often in ways English can only show with its tone of voice. Hebrew labels use “particle” for words such as “not” ([[negative]]), the question marker ([[interrogative-particle]]) and “this” ([[demonstrative-particle]]).

entries.title: Interjection
match: interjection
exclamation=an exclamation
entries.short: A word that is an exclamation on its own: “Oh!”, “Alas!”, “Look!”.

body.p: An interjection stands outside the grammar of the sentence, like a cry. In the New Testament, οὐαί is “woe!” or “how terrible!”, and ἰδού is “look!” or “see!”. Hebrew has הוֹי, “woe!”, and the very common [[hinneh|הִנֵּה, “look!”]], among others.

entries.title: Subject
entries.short: The person or thing a sentence is about: usually the one doing the action. In “Jesus wept”, Jesus is the subject.

body.p: Ask “who or what is doing this?” and the answer is the subject. In “the shepherd calls the sheep”, the shepherd is the subject.

In English the subject usually comes before the verb. In Greek you can tell the subject from its ending, the [[nominative]] case, wherever it stands. In both Greek and Hebrew the verb itself shows who the subject is ([[person]] and [[number]]), so a separate word for “he” or “they” is often left out: λέγει means “he says”.

entries.title: Object
entries.short: The person or thing an action is done to. In “the shepherd calls the sheep”, the sheep are the object.

body.p: Ask “whom or what?” after the verb: “calls whom? the sheep”. That is the direct object. Some verbs also have an indirect object, the person something is given to or done for: in “he gave *them* bread”, “them” is the indirect object.

In Greek the direct object usually has the [[accusative]] ending and the indirect object the [[dative]]. In Hebrew a direct object that is a particular, known one (a name, or a noun with “the” or “my”) often has the small word אֵת in front of it: see [[object-marker|the object marker]].

entries.title: Sentences, clauses and phrases
entries.short: A sentence is a complete thought; a clause is a part of a sentence with its own verb; a phrase is a group of words without one.

body.p: “When the Sabbath was over, they bought spices” is one sentence with two clauses: “when the Sabbath was over” and “they bought spices”. Each clause has its own [[verb]]. A phrase is a group of words that belongs together but has no verb of its own: “in the beginning”, “the word of God”.
Grammar books talk about clauses because the [[mood]] or form of a verb often depends on what kind of clause it is in, such as a clause beginning “so that” or “if”.

entries.title: Person: 1st, 2nd and 3rd
match: person=who is involved: speaker, spoken to, or spoken about
1st=the one speaking or writing: I, we
2nd=the one spoken to: you
3rd=someone or something being talked about: he, she, it, they
first=the one speaking or writing: I, we
second=the one spoken to: you
third=someone or something being talked about: he, she, it, they
entries.short: Who is involved: 1st person is the speaker (I, we), 2nd person is the one spoken to (you), 3rd person is anyone else (he, she, it, they).

body.p: Grammar counts three “persons”:

ul: 1st person: the one speaking or writing, “I” or (with others) “we”;
2nd person: the one being spoken to, “you”;
3rd person: anyone or anything else, “he”, “she”, “it” or “they”.

body.p: Greek and Hebrew verbs show the person with their ending or prefix, so “I” or “they” is usually not written as a separate word. A label such as “3rd singular” means “he, she or it”; “2nd plural” means “you”, speaking to more than one person. Hebrew labels write the words out, “third singular”, and under each word the app shortens it further: see [[pgn]].

English “you” is the same for one person or many. Greek and Hebrew are not, so the label tells you which: the app writes “you (one)” and “you (more than one)”. Older English Bibles kept the difference with “thou” (one) and “ye” (more than one).

entries.title: Number: singular, plural and dual
match: singular=one
plural=more than one
dual=two, a pair
entries.short: Whether a word means one (singular) or more than one (plural). Hebrew also has a form for two (dual).

body.p: English shows number with endings such as “word, words” or “child, children”. Greek and Hebrew do the same, with their own endings: λόγος, “word”, and λόγοι, “words”; דָּבָר, “word”, and דְּבָרִים, “words”.
A verb also has a number, to match its [[subject]]: “he says” is singular, “they say” is plural.
Hebrew has a third number, the dual, for things that come in twos, especially pairs of body parts: יָדַיִם, “hands” (a pair). See [[dual]].

entries.title: Gender: masculine, feminine and neuter
match: masculine=grammatically masculine
feminine=grammatically feminine
neuter=grammatically neither masculine nor feminine
male or female=the same form for either gender
common=the same form for either gender
entries.short: Every Greek and Hebrew noun is grammatically masculine or feminine (and in Greek it can also be neuter). It is a grammar class, not a statement about the thing itself.

body.p: In English only people and animals have a gender (“he”, “she”), and things are “it”. In Greek and Hebrew every noun belongs to a gender class, even words for things and ideas. Greek has three: masculine, feminine and neuter (meaning “neither”). Hebrew has two: masculine and feminine.

Grammatical gender is mostly about word shapes, not about meaning: Greek λόγος, “word”, is masculine; ἀλήθεια, “truth”, is feminine; and τέκνον, “child”, is neuter. For people, though, the gender usually matches.

Gender matters because words that go together must match: an [[adjective]], the [[article|article]] “the” and a pronoun take the same gender as their noun. Verbs show gender too in Hebrew: “you said” is a different word when speaking to a man or to a woman. Where one form serves for both, the label says “male or female”. Grammar books call this “common”, and the short labels write it c, as in 3cp, “they” (see [[pgn]]).

entries.title: Agreement: words that match
entries.short: Words that belong together take matching forms: an adjective matches its noun, and a verb matches its subject.

body.p: In English we say “he walks” but “they walk”: the verb agrees with its subject. Greek and Hebrew do much more of this. An adjective and “the” take the same [[gender]], [[number]] and (in Greek) [[case]] as the noun they belong with: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, “the good shepherd” (literally “the shepherd, the good one”: see [[greek-adjective]]), has four masculine, singular, [[nominative]] words, “the” twice.
Agreement helps you read: it shows which words belong together, even when they are far apart in the sentence.

entries.title: Endings and inflection
entries.short: Changing a word's shape (usually its ending) to show its grammar, as English “walk” becomes “walked” or “walks”.

body.p: English does this a little: “walk, walks, walked, walking”, or “he, him, his”. This changing of a word's shape is called inflection. Greek and Hebrew do it much more. A Greek noun changes its ending to show its [[case]] and number; a Greek verb changes its ending to show who is doing it and when. A Hebrew word adds prefixes and endings, and its vowels shift as it grows.

A table showing all the forms of a word is called a paradigm. Learning the common patterns, rather than every form of every word, is how most of the grammar is learned: the lessons give the tables you need, one at a time.
The part of the word that carries its meaning is the [[stem]]. What is added to it is a prefix (at the front) or an ending, also called a suffix (at the back).

entries.title: Stem
entries.short: The part of a word that carries its meaning, to which endings are added: walk- in walks, walked, walking; λυ- in λύω, λύεις, λύομεν.

body.p: Take away the ending from a word, and what is left is its stem. In λόγος, “word”, the stem is λογ- and the ending is -ος. Different endings on the same stem give different forms: λόγου, “of a word”, λόγῳ, “to a word”.

In Hebrew grammar the word “stem” is also used for something else: the seven or so patterns a Hebrew verb can follow, such as [[qal]] or [[piel]]. See [[stems]]. The three consonants underneath a Hebrew word are called its [[root]].

entries.title: Tense: time
match: past=in the past
present=in the present
future=still to come
entries.short: The form of a verb that shows when something happens: in the past, the present or the future.

body.p: In English, “I go”, “I went” and “I will go” differ in tense. Greek grammar uses the word tense for each set of verb forms ([[present]], [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]], [[future]], [[aorist]], [[perfect-greek|perfect]], [[pluperfect]]), but these forms show more than time: they also show how the action is viewed, which is called [[aspect]].

Hebrew verbs are even less about time. Their two main forms (see [[perfect-hebrew]] and [[imperfect-hebrew]]) mostly show whether an action is seen as complete or not. The time comes from the context. That is why STEPBible's Hebrew labels say “past/present” or “future/present”: [[time-in-labels|either may be right]].

entries.title: Aspect: how an action is viewed
entries.short: Whether an action is seen as a whole event or as something going on. “He walked to town” views it whole; “he was walking to town” views it in progress.

body.p: English can say the same event two ways. “Jesus wept” presents the weeping as a single fact. “Jesus was weeping” takes us inside it while it goes on. That difference, between viewing an action from outside as a whole and from inside as it unfolds, is called aspect.

Greek shows aspect in its verb forms. The [[aorist]] presents an action as a whole; the [[present]] and [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]] present it as ongoing or repeated; the [[perfect-greek|perfect]] presents a finished action whose result still stands. Hebrew's main verb forms are also mostly about aspect: complete ([[perfect-hebrew]]) or not complete ([[imperfect-hebrew]]).

Scholars still discuss exactly how much Greek and Hebrew verb forms say about time and how much about aspect. For reading, the safe rule is: let the context decide the time, and let the form tell you how the writer views the action.

entries.title: Voice: active, middle and passive
entries.short: Whether the subject does the action (active: “he taught”), receives it (passive: “he was taught”), or acts for or on itself (middle).

body.p: “The shepherd *calls* the sheep” is active: the subject does the action. “The sheep *are called* by the shepherd” is passive: the subject receives it. Voice is the name for this difference.

Greek has a third voice, the [[middle]], in which the subject is involved in the action in some special way, often doing it for itself. In Hebrew, active and passive (and reflexive, “doing it to oneself”) are part of the verb's [[stems|stem]] rather than a separate voice.

entries.title: Active
match: active=the subject does the action
entries.short: The subject does the action: “he taught”, “they see”.

body.p: Most verbs, most of the time, are active. In “God loved the world”, God does the loving. In Hebrew labels, “active” is part of the [[stems|stem]] description: [[qal]] is “simple, active”, and [[hiphil]] “causative/declarative, active” (making someone do something, or declaring something so). Its partner is the [[passive]].

entries.title: Passive
match: passive=the subject receives the action
entries.short: The subject receives the action instead of doing it: “he was taught”, “it is written”.

body.p: In “it is written”, nobody is named as the writer: the passive puts the thing written in the place of the subject. In English we build the passive with “be” and a verb form: “was taken”, “is written”, “will be saved”. Greek has passive endings. Hebrew has passive [[stems]]: the [[niphal]], [[pual]] and [[hophal]].
Sometimes a passive with no one named hides a reference to God: “they will be comforted” ([MAT 5:4]) means God will comfort them. Grammar books call this the divine passive.

entries.title: Mood
entries.short: The form of a verb that shows how the speaker presents the action: as a fact, a possibility, a wish or a command.

body.p: “You go” states a fact. “Go!” is a command. “If you were to go” is a possibility. These differences are called mood.

Greek has four moods: [[indicative]] (statements and questions), [[subjunctive]] (what may happen), [[optative]] (wishes) and [[imperative]] (commands). [[grammar-labels|Grammar labels]] also put the [[infinitive]] (“to go”) and the [[participle]] (“going”) in the same place, although they work differently: they have no [[person]] (“I”, “you”, “he”). Hebrew has forms for commands and wishes too: [[imperative]], [[jussive]] and [[cohortative]].

entries.title: Indicative
match: indicative=a statement of fact (or a question)
entries.short: The ordinary form of a verb for saying that something is, was or will be so: “he went”, “God is love”.

body.p: Most verbs in a story are indicative. They state facts, or ask about them: “did he go?”. In Greek, only the indicative shows time clearly: it is the only form that has an [[augment]] for the past.
STEPBible's Hebrew labels add “indicative” in brackets to show that a form is used as a plain statement, as opposed to a wish ([[jussive]], [[cohortative]]).

entries.title: Imperative: commands
match: imperative=a command or request
entries.short: The form of a verb for telling someone to do something: “Come!”, “Listen!”, “Love your neighbour.”

body.p: A command speaks to someone, so it is usually [[person|2nd person]]: “you, do this!”. Greek also has a 3rd person imperative, which English translates “let him…” or “let it…”: γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου, “let your will be done”.
In Greek the [[aspect]] still matters in a command. An [[aorist]] imperative tells someone to do a thing; a [[present]] imperative often tells them to keep doing it, or to make it their habit.

Hebrew imperatives are always 2nd person. Hebrew commands for “let him” or “let us” use the [[jussive]] and [[cohortative]]. A command not to do something is not made with the imperative in either language: see [[prohibition]].

entries.title: Commands not to do something
entries.short: “Do not…”. Greek says it with μή, Hebrew with לֹא or אַל, each with particular verb forms.

body.p: In Greek, “do not” is μή, never οὐ, with a [[present]] [[imperative]] or an [[aorist]] [[subjunctive]]. With the present imperative it sometimes means “stop doing” or “don't make a habit of it”: μὴ φοβοῦ, “do not be afraid”. With the aorist subjunctive it forbids the action as a whole: μὴ φοβηθῇς.
In Hebrew, לֹא with the [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] gives a lasting command: לֹא תִּרְצָח, “you shall not murder”. אַל with the [[jussive]] gives a more immediate “don't”.

entries.title: Infinitive
match: infinitive=the “to …” form of a verb
entries.short: The form of a verb that names the action itself, without a person: “to go”, “to love”.

body.p: “I want *to go*” and “*To love* is to give” use infinitives. (English “going”, in “going is hard”, can do the same job.) An infinitive has no [[person]] or [[number]]: it names the action, a little like a noun.

[[greek-infinitive|Greek infinitives]] have their own endings, such as -ειν or -σαι, and can even take “the” in front of them. Hebrew has two infinitives with different uses: the [[infinitive-construct]], used like “to go” or “when he went”, and the [[infinitive-absolute]], often used to strengthen another verb.

entries.title: Participle
match: participle=a verb used like an adjective or a noun: “going”, “one who goes”
entries.short: A verb used as an adjective or noun: “the *sleeping* child”, “the one *who believes*”, “*having said* this”.

body.p: English participles end in “-ing” or “-ed”: “a *burning* bush”, “the *written* word”. They are part verb (they have a [[tense]] and a [[voice]]) and part adjective (they describe a noun).

Greek uses participles constantly, much more than English, and they have the endings of an [[adjective]]. English often has to turn them into a whole clause: ὁ πιστεύων, literally “the believing”, is “the one who believes”. See [[greek-participle]]. Hebrew uses participles for ongoing actions and for people who do something: see [[hebrew-participle]].

entries.title: Comparative and superlative
match: comparative=“more …”, or “-er”
superlative=“most …”, or “-est”
entries.short: The forms that compare: “greater” is comparative, “greatest” is superlative.

body.p: English adds “-er” and “-est”, or “more” and “most”: great, greater, greatest. Greek has endings for the same: μείζων, “greater”, from μέγας, “great”. In the New Testament the comparative often does the work of the superlative too, so μείζων can mean “greatest” ([MAT 18:1]).
Hebrew has no separate forms for this. It says “greater than” with the preposition מִן, “from”: “good *from* him” means “better than him”.

entries.title: Number words: one, two, first
match: numeral=a number word
numerical=a number word (one, two, three)
numerical position=a number for position in order (first, second, third)
entries.short: Words for numbers. Cardinal numbers count (one, two, three); ordinal numbers put things in order (first, second, third).

body.p: Number words are a kind of [[adjective]]. In Greek, one to four change their endings; most larger numbers never change ([[indeclinable]]). In Hebrew, numbers behave in surprising ways: from three to ten, a masculine noun takes a number word with a feminine-looking ending, and the other way round.
STEPBible's Hebrew labels call counting numbers “numerical” and order numbers “numerical position”. The app writes them as “number” and “number (order)”.

entries.title: Not: negative words
match: negative=a “not” word, or a word with “not” built in (no one, never)
not=the word “not”
entries.short: Words for “not”, “no” and “never”. Greek has two, οὐ and μή; Hebrew has לֹא and אַל among others.

body.p: Greek has two ways of saying “not”. οὐ (οὐκ before a vowel, οὐχ before a [[breathing|rough breathing]], an h sound) denies a fact: “he is not here”. μή is used with wishes, commands, conditions and most forms that are not the [[indicative]]: “do not be afraid”. A question that begins with οὐ expects the answer “yes”; one that begins with μή expects “no”.
Hebrew uses לֹא for most statements and lasting commands, and אַל for urgent ones (see [[prohibition]]). Other words such as אֵין, “there is not”, and בְּלִי, “without”, also say “not”.
Some Greek words have the “not” built in, such as οὐδείς, “no one”, and μηδέ, “and not”. STEPBible's labels mark these “negative” too.

entries.title: The Greek alphabet
entries.short: Greek has twenty-four letters, seven of them vowels. English took many of its letters from it, through Latin.

body.p: The word “alphabet” comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta. Many Greek letters look and sound like ours: α a, β b, κ k, τ t. Some look like ours but stand for other sounds: η is a long e, ρ is r, ν is n, χ is kh. And a few are new shapes: γ, δ, θ, λ, ξ, π, σ, φ, ψ, ω.
The [[#/alphabet/grc|Letters tab]] shows every letter with its name, its sound in both pronunciations ([[erasmian]] and [[restored-koine]]), and examples you can hear.

entries.title: Greek vowels: long, short and pairs
entries.short: Greek has seven vowels: α ε η ι ο υ ω. η and ω are always long, ε and ο always short, and α, ι and υ can be either. Two vowels together often make one sound, such as ου, oo.

body.p: The seven vowels come in two kinds. ε and η are a short and a long e; ο and ω a short and a long o. α, ι and υ can be long or short, and the spelling doesn't show which. Length matters for the [[accents]] and for the shape of endings, though the app's voices don't hold long vowels any longer than short ones.
Some pairs of vowels are said as one sound, a diphthong (“two sounds”). In the app's [[erasmian|Erasmian]] pronunciation:

In [[restored-koine|Restored Koine]] most of these had become single vowels by the first century: the [[letters-tab|Letters tab]] shows both side by side. Two dots over the second vowel ([[diaeresis]]) mean the pair is said as two sounds after all, and a small ι under a long vowel ([[iota-subscript]]) is not said at all.

entries.title: Breathing marks
entries.short: A small mark like an apostrophe over a word's first vowel. A rough breathing (῾) adds an h sound; a smooth breathing (᾿) adds nothing.

body.p: Almost every Greek word that begins with a vowel has a breathing mark on it. The rough breathing, curved like an opening quotation mark, means the word starts with an h: ὁ is “ho”, ἁμαρτία is “hamartia”. The smooth breathing, curved the other way, means no h: ἐν is “en”.

A few rules: a word starting with ρ nearly always has a rough breathing (ῥῆμα), which isn't said, and a word starting with υ always does (υἱός). A few Aramaic words written in Greek letters, such as Αββα, have no breathing at all. When a word starts with a pair of vowels, the mark sits on the second: αὐτός, εἰς. On a capital letter it stands in front: Ἰησοῦς.

In the [[erasmian|Erasmian]] pronunciation the h is said. In [[restored-koine]] it is not, because by the first century the h sound had dropped out of everyday Greek, and the voice can't say it either way.

entries.title: Accents
entries.short: Small marks over a vowel (´ ` ῀) that show which syllable to stress. They were added by later scholars, and today all three simply mean “stress here”.

body.p: Greek has three accents. The acute (´) rises to the right, the grave (`) falls to the right, and the circumflex (῀) is a small wave. In ancient Greek they showed a rise and fall of pitch, a little like a tune. By New Testament times Greek was stressed like English, and in both of the app's pronunciations each accent just marks the stressed syllable: λόγος is LO-gos, ἀγάπη is a-GA-pay.
An acute on the last syllable of a word turns into a grave when another word follows without a pause: τόν becomes τὸν in τὸν λόγον. It is the same word.
Accents sometimes tell apart words that are otherwise spelt alike: εἰ, “if”, and εἶ, “you are”; ἡ, “the”, ἥ, “who”, and ἤ, “or”.

The earliest manuscripts of the New Testament have no accents. Scholars in Alexandria had invented them earlier, but scribes only began to write them regularly centuries later. The accents in printed Bibles come from that later tradition.

entries.title: Words with no accent of their own
entries.short: A few short words lean on their neighbour and have no accent of their own: μου, “my”, and τις, “someone”, lean back; ὁ, ἐν and οὐ lean forward.

body.p: Some short Greek words are said together with the word next to them, as if they were part of it. Enclitics, such as μου, σου, τις and often ἐστιν, lean on the word before. They usually lose their accent, and sometimes give an extra one to the word they lean on: ὁ λόγος μου, “my word”; ἄνθρωπός τις, “a certain man”. Proclitics, such as ὁ, ἡ, ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ and οὐ, lean on the word after, and have no accent.
That is why the app's respellings show these words without a stressed syllable, and why ἄνθρωπός, before τις, carries two accents.

entries.title: Iota subscript
entries.short: A small ι written under α, η or ω (ᾳ ῃ ῳ). It is not said today, but it often marks the [[dative]] case.

body.p: Once these were long α, η and ω followed by a real ι, but the ι stopped being said, and scribes later wrote it as a tiny letter underneath. It doesn't change the pronunciation, but it matters for reading, because it often marks the [[dative]] case: τῷ λόγῳ, “to the word”; τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, “on the day”.

entries.title: Diaeresis: two dots
entries.short: Two dots over a vowel (ϊ ϋ) mean it is said on its own, not as part of a pair: Ἠσαΐας, “Isaiah”, is said ay-sa-EE-as.

body.p: Pairs of vowels such as αι and ευ are usually said as one sound. When they are not, the second vowel has two dots: Ἠσαΐας is four syllables, not three. You will see this mostly in names taken from Hebrew, such as Ἠσαΐας and Μωϋσῆς, “Moses”.

entries.title: Elision: a dropped vowel
entries.short: A short vowel at the end of a word is often dropped before a word starting with a vowel, and an apostrophe marks the place: δι’ αὐτοῦ, “through him”, for διά αὐτοῦ.

body.p: Greek avoids two vowels meeting across words, so it often drops the first one: ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ for ἀπό ἐμοῦ, “from me”; δι’ αὐτοῦ for διὰ αὐτοῦ. If the next word has a rough [[breathing|breathing]], the consonant before the apostrophe may change too: ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ, “from himself”, for ἀπὸ ἑαυτοῦ.
The SBL Greek New Testament writes the apostrophe as ʼ. The meaning is exactly that of the full word, and the app's dictionary lists it under the full form.

entries.title: Crasis: two words merged into one
entries.short: Two words run together into one, with a mark showing the join: κἀγώ is καί + ἐγώ, “and I”.

body.p: Crasis (Greek for “mixing”) merges two words into one. In the New Testament it is mostly καί with a word starting with a vowel: κἀγώ, “and I”, κἀκεῖνος, “and that one”, κἄν, “even if”. The mark over the join looks like a smooth [[breathing|breathing]], but it marks the merge. The app shows these words as joined from two, with both parts' meanings.

entries.title: Movable ν
entries.short: Some word endings can take an extra ν before a vowel or at a pause: ἐστί or ἐστίν, “is”. The word is the same either way.

body.p: To avoid two vowels meeting, Greek adds ν to certain endings that end in a vowel, especially -σι, -ε and ἐστί: λέγουσι or λέγουσιν, “they say”. Writers and scribes didn't always follow the rule, and the SBL text often has the ν even before a consonant. It never changes the meaning.

entries.title: Final sigma: σ and ς
entries.short: The letter s has two shapes: σ inside a word and ς at the end. They are the same letter.

body.p: λόγος has both: σ is never written at the end of a word, and ς never inside one. The capital is Σ. Ancient manuscripts mostly wrote a third shape, like a C, everywhere, and some printed editions copy it. The [[words-tab|Words tab]] treats all of them as the same letter when you search.

entries.title: Greek punctuation
entries.short: Greek uses . and , as English does, a raised dot · for a pause like a colon or semicolon, and ; for a question mark.

body.p: The Greek question mark looks like an English semicolon: τίς ἐστιν; “who is he?”. The raised dot · marks a longer pause than a comma: often it comes just before someone's words, where English would put a colon.

The first manuscripts had almost no punctuation, and often no spaces between words. Modern editors add it, and editions sometimes punctuate differently. Occasionally that changes how a verse is read: [JHN 1:3] and [JHN 1:4] can be divided in two ways, and translations differ.

entries.title: Capital letters in the Greek text
entries.short: The Greek text uses capitals for names, for the start of a paragraph and for the start of someone's words, but not for every sentence.

body.p: English starts each sentence with a capital. The SBL Greek New Testament doesn't: a new sentence in the middle of a paragraph starts with a small letter. Capitals mark names (Ἰησοῦς, Γαλιλαία), the first word of a paragraph, and the first word of a quotation: Ἐγώ εἰμι, “I am”, when someone starts speaking.

entries.title: Double brackets ⟦ ⟧
entries.short: Double square brackets mark passages that most scholars think were added to the text after it was first written, such as Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11.

body.p: Some passages are missing from the oldest and best manuscripts but are found in many later ones. The SBL Greek New Testament prints the two longest of these, the longer ending of Mark ([MRK 16:9]) and the story of the woman caught in adultery ([JHN 7:53]), between ⟦ and ⟧, and the short ending of Mark after [MRK 16:8] too. The Reader puts a note wherever they appear.
The brackets don't say the passages are untrue or should be ignored. They say that the editors think they were not part of the book as first written. Many Bibles print them with a similar note.

entries.title: Paragraphs in the Greek text
entries.short: The Greek text is divided into paragraphs by its editors, and the Reader's running-text layout shows them.

body.p: Like punctuation, paragraphs are the editors' choice, not the writers'. The SBL Greek New Testament marks where each paragraph begins. In the Reader's running-text layout these become the paragraphs on the page. In the word-by-word layout each verse stands on its own, so paragraphs don't show. The Hebrew text has its own paragraph marks: see [[petuha-setuma]].

entries.title: Letters used as numbers
entries.short: In the [[septuagint]] some numbers are written with letters and a mark: β᾽ is two, ι᾽ ten, ιδ᾽ fourteen. The app shows each one's value and reads it as a number.

body.p: Greeks used their letters as numbers: α is one, β two, γ three and so on, ι ten, κ twenty, ρ a hundred. A small mark after the letters shows that they are a number, not a word: ιδ᾽ is ten plus four, fourteen. The New Testament writes numbers out as words, but Swete's Septuagint uses these figures in many lists. When you tap one, the app gives its value, and the Listen button says the number as a Greek word in the right form.

entries.title: Case: what a noun's ending shows
entries.short: The case is the form of a Greek noun (and of “the”, adjectives and pronouns) that shows its job in the sentence: subject, object, “of”, “to” and so on.

body.p: English shows a noun's job mostly by word order. “The dog bit the man” and “the man bit the dog” have the same words in a different order. Greek shows the job with the ending instead, so the words can come in almost any order.
English still has a little of this in its pronouns: “he” is the subject (he saw her), “him” is the object (she saw him), and “his” means “of him”. Greek does the same with every noun.
Greek has five cases:

ul: [[nominative]]: the subject, “*the shepherd* calls”;
[[genitive]]: “of”, “*the shepherd's* voice”;
[[dative]]: “to” or “for”, “he gave it *to the shepherd*”;
[[accusative]]: the object, “they saw *the shepherd*”;
[[vocative]]: calling someone, “*Shepherd*, come!”.

body.p: The endings for each case depend on the noun's [[gender]], its [[number]], and which family of nouns it belongs to (its [[declension]]).

entries.title: Nominative
match: nominative=the subject case
entries.short: The case of the subject, the person or thing doing the action: “*the Word* was”. Dictionaries list nouns in the nominative.

body.p: In [JHN 1:1], ὁ λόγος, “the Word”, is nominative, because it is the [[subject]]: the Word was. The nominative is also used after “is” or “was” for what the subject is: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος, “the Word was God”. Here both θεός and λόγος are nominative (θεός is written θεὸς before another word: see [[accents]]), and the [[greek-article|word “the”]] shows which is the subject.
Names and titles in lists, headings and greetings are often in the nominative too: Παῦλος, “Paul”, at the start of a letter.

entries.title: Genitive
match: genitive=the “of” case
entries.short: The “of” case: it shows whose something is or what it is connected with: “the word *of God*”, “*Jesus'* disciples”.

body.p: The genitive usually describes or narrows down another noun, and English translates it with “of” or with “'s”: ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, “the word of God”. It can show belonging (the house of Peter), source (the gospel of God), what something is made of, or what kind of thing it is (the body of sin: a sinful body).
The genitive is also used after some [[preposition|prepositions]], such as ἐκ, “out of”, ἀπό, “from”, and διά, “through”, and to compare (“greater than him”).
Greek grammars name many kinds of genitive. The context, not the ending, decides which one fits: “the love of God” can be God's love for us or our love for God.

entries.title: Dative
match: dative=the “to” or “for” case
entries.short: The “to” or “for” case: the person something is given or said to, and also “with” or “by”: “he said *to them*”.

body.p: The dative marks the indirect [[object]]: εἶπεν αὐτοῖς, “he said to them”. It is also used for the means by which something is done (“by grace”, “with water”), for place (“in the house”) and time (“on the third day”).

Many prepositions take the dative, especially ἐν, “in”, and σύν, “with”. Some verbs take their object in the dative instead of the [[accusative]], such as πιστεύω, “I believe (in)”, and ἀκολουθέω, “I follow”.

entries.title: Accusative
match: accusative=the object case
entries.short: The case of the direct object, the person or thing the action is done to: “God loved *the world*”.

body.p: In “God loved the world”, the world is what was loved, so in Greek it is accusative: τὸν κόσμον. The accusative also follows some prepositions, especially εἰς, “into”, and πρός, “to” or “with”, and it can show how long something lasts (“for three days”).
Neuter nouns use the same form for the [[nominative]] and accusative, so the context has to show which is meant.

entries.title: Vocative
match: vocative=the case for calling someone
entries.short: The case for calling or speaking to someone: “*Lord*, teach us to pray”.

body.p: When someone is spoken to directly, their name or title is in the vocative: κύριε, “Lord!”, πάτερ, “Father!”. Older English used “O”: “O Lord”. Many nouns have no separate vocative and use the [[nominative]] form instead, sometimes with “the”: ὁ πατήρ, “Father!”.

entries.title: Declensions: the three noun families
entries.short: Greek nouns fall into three families, each with its own set of case endings. The family is called a declension.

body.p: All Greek nouns use the same five [[case|cases]], but not the same endings. There are three sets of endings, and every noun follows one of them:

ul: [[first-declension]]: mostly feminine nouns ending in -α or -η, such as ἡμέρα, “day”, and γραφή, “scripture”;
[[second-declension]]: mostly masculine nouns ending in -ος, such as λόγος, and neuter nouns in -ον, such as τέκνον, “child”;
[[third-declension]]: everything else, such as σάρξ, “flesh”, πατήρ, “father”, and ὄνομα, “name”.

body.p: [[grammar-labels|Grammar labels]] don't say which family a noun belongs to: it doesn't change the meaning. But knowing the families lets you recognise a case ending you have never seen on that word. Dictionaries help by giving the [[genitive]] ending after the noun: λόγος, -ου; σάρξ, σαρκός.

entries.title: First declension
entries.short: The family of nouns that end in -α or -η, mostly feminine: ἡμέρα, γραφή, δόξα. A few masculine ones end in -ης or -ας.

body.p: Most first declension nouns are feminine, and end in -η or -α in the dictionary: ἀγάπη, “love”, καρδία, “heart”, δόξα, “glory”. Their endings have η or α in the singular and are the same in the plural for all of them: -αι, -ων, -αις, -ας.
A small group are masculine and end in -ης or -ας: προφήτης, “prophet”, μαθητής, “disciple”. They use the same plural.

entries.title: Second declension
entries.short: The family of masculine nouns in -ος, such as λόγος, and neuter nouns in -ον, such as ἔργον, “work”.

body.p: This is the family most learners meet first. Most nouns ending in -ος are masculine, but a few are feminine, such as ὁδός, “road”, and ἔρημος, “desert”. The article shows which: ἡ ὁδός.
Neuter nouns end in -ον, and their plural ends in -α: ἔργον, “work”, ἔργα, “works”. For neuter nouns the [[nominative]] and [[accusative]] are always the same.

entries.title: Third declension
entries.short: The family of all other nouns, whose stem often only shows in the other cases: σάρξ, “flesh”, σαρκός, “of flesh”.

body.p: Third declension nouns have many different endings in the [[nominative]] singular, which makes them harder to recognise: σάρξ, πατήρ, ὄνομα, πόλις, πνεῦμα. Their real [[stem]] shows in the other cases: σαρκ-, πατρ-, ὀνοματ-.

That is why dictionaries give the [[genitive]] with every noun. The genitive singular of these nouns usually ends in -ος: σαρκός, πατρός, ὀνόματος. The other endings are fairly regular: the [[dative]] singular ends in -ι, the [[accusative]] in -α or -ν, and the dative plural in -σι (or -σιν: see [[movable-nu]]).

entries.title: Neuter
entries.short: The third Greek gender, meaning “neither” masculine nor feminine. Neuter nouns use the same form for subject and object.

body.p: Neuter nouns include many things and ideas (ἔργον, “work”, πνεῦμα, “spirit”), but also τέκνον and παιδίον, “child”, because grammatical [[gender]] is about word shape, not meaning.

Two rules help with neuter words. Their [[nominative]] and [[accusative]] forms are always the same. And a neuter plural subject often takes a singular verb: τὰ πρόβατα… ἀκούει, “the sheep hear” ([JHN 10:3]).

entries.title: The Greek article: ὁ, ἡ, τό
entries.short: Greek's word for “the”. It changes its ending to match its noun in gender, number and case, and it is used more often than English “the”.

body.p: The article has the same ending patterns as nouns of the first two families, so knowing it helps you read the ending of the noun after it. It has no accent in four of its forms (ὁ, ἡ, οἱ, αἱ), and starts with τ in all the others.

Greek uses the article in places where English doesn't. It often comes before names (ὁ Ἰησοῦς, “Jesus”) and before words for ideas (ἡ ἀγάπη, “love”), and English leaves it out. Where Greek has no article, English sometimes adds “a” and sometimes nothing.

The article can also turn almost anything into a noun: τὰ ἄνω, “the things above”, ὁ πιστεύων, “the one who believes”. And it can stand for a person on its own: ὁ δέ, “and he”. Whether a noun has an article or not can matter for its meaning, and such places, like [JHN 1:1], are much discussed.

entries.title: How Greek adjectives work
entries.short: A Greek adjective takes the same gender, number and case as its noun. Where it stands next to “the” decides whether it means “the good man” or “the man is good”.

body.p: A Greek adjective has endings like a noun's. It copies the [[gender]], [[number]] and [[case]] of the noun it describes, which is called [[agreement]].

Its place matters. When the adjective has the article “the” directly in front of it, it describes the noun: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, or ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός, both mean “the good man”. When the article is in front of the noun only, the adjective says something about it, as a statement: ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός, “the man is good”.
An adjective with “the” and no noun works as a noun: ὁ ἀγαθός, “the good man”, or τὸ ἀγαθόν, “what is good”.

entries.title: Indeclinable
match: indeclinable=never changes its ending
letter=the name of a letter of the alphabet
entries.short: A word that never changes its ending, whatever its case: many Hebrew names, such as Ἀβραάμ, and most numbers.

body.p: Most Greek nouns change their ending to show their [[case]]. Some never do. They are called indeclinable (they can't be “declined”, meaning put through their cases). Many are names from the Old Testament, written in Greek letters: Ἀβραάμ, Ἰσραήλ, Ἰερουσαλήμ. Numbers above four are usually indeclinable too: δώδεκα, “twelve”.

With these words the case has to come from the rest of the sentence: from the article in front of it, a preposition, or the sense. The grammar label still gives the case, as worked out from the context.
The letters Alpha and Omega in [REV 1:8] are labelled “indeclinable letter”: they are the names of letters, used as nouns.

entries.title: Transcribed words
match: transcribed from hebrew=a Hebrew word written in Greek letters
transcribed from aramaic=an Aramaic word written in Greek letters
transcribed=written in Greek letters from another language
entries.short: A Hebrew or Aramaic word kept as it was and written in Greek letters, such as ἀμήν, “amen”, or Ταλιθα, “little girl”.

body.p: Some words were taken into Greek without being translated, just as English Bibles keep “amen” and “hallelujah”. They are written in Greek letters but are really Hebrew or Aramaic: ἀμήν, “truly”; ὡσαννά, “hosanna”, from a Hebrew cry meaning “save, please”; ῥαββί, “my teacher”; πάσχα, “Passover”.

Most of them never change their ending ([[indeclinable]]). STEPBible's labels say “transcribed from Hebrew” or “transcribed from Aramaic”. The Aramaic words of Jesus are explained in [[aramaic-language]].

entries.title: Contracted form
match: contracted form=a form marked as shortened in the tagging
contracted=a form marked as shortened in the tagging
entries.short: A label STEPBible puts on a few words. In the New Testament it is used only for πρεσβύτερος, “elder”, which began as a word meaning “older”.

body.p: The tagging system marks some nouns as a “contracted form”. In the New Testament as the app has it, the {{elder}} words with this label are all forms of πρεσβύτερος, “elder”, as in the elders of the church or the elders of the people. The word is the [[comparative|comparative]] of an older word for “old man”, so it first meant “older”, and became a title. For reading, treat it as a normal noun of the [[second-declension]].

In the same tagging system, the ending -C on an adjective means comparative, and that may be what was meant here. Contraction in Greek usually means two vowels merging into one, as in the [[contract-verbs]].

entries.title: Attic Greek form
match: attic greek form=an older spelling from the Greek of Athens
attic=an older spelling from the Greek of Athens
entries.short: A form spelt the older way, as in the classical Greek of Athens, rather than the usual Koine way.

body.p: Koine grew out of Attic, the Greek of Athens in its golden age. Most Attic forms had changed by the time of the New Testament, but a few writers kept some of the older ones. STEPBible marks such forms “Attic Greek form”. The example below, ἠδυνήθητε, “you were able”, has an η at the front where Koine more often wrote ε (see [[augment]]). The meaning is the same.

entries.title: Greek personal pronouns
entries.short: The Greek words for “I”, “you”, “he”, “she”, “it”, “we” and “they”: ἐγώ, σύ, αὐτός, ἡμεῖς, ὑμεῖς. They change their ending for case like nouns.

body.p: Greek verbs already show who is doing the action, so a word for “I” or “you” is often left out. When a writer does use one, it is usually for emphasis or contrast: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς, “*I* am the bread of life”.

The forms change with [[case]]: ἐγώ is “I”, με is “me”, μου is “of me” or “my”, μοι is “to me”. The commonest way to say “my” or “his” is the [[genitive]] of the pronoun after the noun: ὁ λόγος μου, “my word”, literally “the word of me”.

αὐτός does three jobs. On its own it means “he”, “she” or “it” (αὐτοῦ, “his”). Between “the” and its noun it means “same”: τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, “the same Spirit”. Outside them, with no “the” of its own, it means “himself”: αὐτὸς ὁ θεός, “God himself”.

entries.title: Possessive pronoun
match: possessive=a word for “my”, “your”, “our”
entries.short: Greek words for “my”, “your”, “our”, such as ἐμός and σός. They are rarer than the [[genitive]] of “I” or “you”.

body.p: The full set is ἐμός, σός, ἡμέτερος and ὑμέτερος. Most often, though, Greek says “my” with μου, the [[genitive]] of ἐγώ: ὁ πατήρ μου, “my father”. Sometimes it uses a separate word that works like an [[adjective]], and STEPBible's labels call it a possessive pronoun. It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμή, “my joy”, is feminine because χαρά is. These words are often a little emphatic: “*my* joy”.

entries.title: Reflexive pronoun
match: reflexive=a word for “-self”, pointing back to the subject
entries.short: A word for “myself”, “yourself”, “himself”: ἐμαυτοῦ, σεαυτοῦ, ἑαυτοῦ. It points back to the subject of its own clause.

body.p: In “he humbled himself”, “himself” is the same person as the subject. Greek uses a reflexive pronoun here: ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν ([PHP 2:8]). Reflexive pronouns have no [[nominative]], because they are never the subject.

The labels say “1st” for “myself”, “2nd” for “yourself”, “3rd” for “himself, herself, itself, themselves”. In the plural ἑαυτῶν can serve for all three persons: “ourselves”, “yourselves”, “themselves”.

entries.title: Reciprocal pronoun
match: reciprocal=“one another”
entries.short: The word for “one another”, ἀλλήλων. It is always plural.

body.p: ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, “love one another” ([JHN 13:34]). Like a [[reflexive|reflexive]] pronoun it has no [[nominative]]: it is never the subject. It is one of the commonest words of the New Testament letters, which have much to say about how believers treat one another.

entries.title: Demonstrative pronoun
match: demonstrative=“this” or “that”: a pointing word
this/that=a word for “this” or “that”
entries.short: A pointing word: “this”, “that”, “these”, “those”. In Greek, οὗτος is “this” and ἐκεῖνος is “that”.

body.p: οὗτος points to something near, or just mentioned: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου, “this is my Son”. ἐκεῖνος points to something further away, or to someone other than the main person: “that day”, “he”.

A demonstrative next to a noun comes before “the” or after the noun, never between them: οὗτος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, “this man”. That is the opposite of an ordinary [[greek-adjective|adjective]]. Hebrew has demonstratives too: see [[demonstrative-particle]].

entries.title: Relative pronoun
match: relative=“who”, “which”, “that”, joining a clause to a noun
entries.short: “Who”, “which” or “that”, introducing a clause that describes a noun: “the man *who* came”. In Greek: ὅς, ἥ, ὅ.

body.p: In “the word *which* I spoke”, “which” begins a clause describing “the word”. Greek's relative pronoun takes its [[gender]] and [[number]] from the noun it refers back to, but its [[case]] from its own job in its own clause: ὁ λόγος ὃν ἐλάλησα, “the word that I spoke” ([JHN 12:48]): ὅν is masculine like λόγος, and [[accusative]] because it is what was spoken.

Its forms look like the article's with a rough [[breathing|breathing]] and an accent: ὅς, ἥ, ὅ, οὗ, ᾧ, ὅν, ἥν. Don't confuse ἥ, “who” (feminine), with ἡ, “the”, or ἤ, “or”: the marks tell them apart. ὅστις is a related word meaning “whoever” or “who indeed”.

entries.title: Interrogative: question words
match: interrogative=a question word: who? what? why?
question word=a word that asks a question
entries.short: Question words: “who?”, “what?”, “why?”, “how?”. In Greek τίς is “who?” and τί is “what?” or “why?”.

body.p: τίς and τί always carry an acute accent (´) on the ι, which never turns into a grave (see [[accents]]). That is how you tell them apart from [[indefinite]] τις and τι, “someone” and “something”, which usually have none. Greek also has question adverbs and particles: πῶς, “how?”, ποῦ, “where?”, πότε, “when?”.

A question in Greek ends with ; which looks like an English semicolon: see [[greek-punctuation]]. In Hebrew a question can start with מִי, “who?”, מָה, “what?”, or the [[interrogative-particle|question prefix]] הֲ.

entries.title: Indefinite pronoun
match: indefinite=“someone”, “something”, “a certain”
entries.short: τις and τι: “someone”, “something”, “a certain”. They look like τίς, “who?”, but usually have no accent.

body.p: With a noun, τις means “a certain”: ἄνθρωπός τις, “a certain man”. On its own it means “someone” or “anyone”: εἴ τις, “if anyone”. It rarely comes first in its clause, and it [[enclitic|leans on the word before it]], so it usually has no accent of its own, or passes one back to that word.

entries.title: Correlative pronoun
match: correlative=a word of amount or kind: “as much as”, “such as”, “so great”
entries.short: Words for amount or kind that come in matching sets: ὅσος, “as much as”, τοσοῦτος, “so much”, οἷος, “such as”, πόσος, “how much?”.

body.p: These words come in families that answer each other: πόσος, “how much?”, τοσοῦτος, “so much”, ὅσος, “as much as”.
