STEPBible's labels call them correlatives, and call the [[interrogative|question words]] among them (such as πόσος) “correlative or interrogative”. They change their endings like adjectives.

entries.title: How a Greek verb is built
entries.short: A Greek verb is a stem with pieces added: often something at the front for the past, then the stem, then an ending that shows who is doing it.

body.p: Take ἐπιστεύσαμεν, “we believed”. It breaks into ἐ- (a mark of the past, the [[augment]]), πιστευ- (the stem, “believe”), -σα- (the sign of the [[aorist]]) and -μεν (“we”). Each piece tells you something, and the grammar label lists what they add up to:

ul: [[tense]]: [[present]], [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]], [[future]], [[aorist]], [[perfect-greek|perfect]] or [[pluperfect]], which shows the [[aspect]] (and, in statements, the time);
[[voice]]: [[active]], [[middle]] or [[passive]];
[[mood]]: [[indicative]], [[subjunctive]], [[optative]], [[imperative]], or one of the forms that are not moods, the [[infinitive]] and [[participle]];
[[person]] and [[number]]: who is doing it.

body.p: So “Verb aorist active indicative 1st plural” describes ἐπιστεύσαμεν exactly. A participle's label gives a [[case]], number and gender instead of a person, because it works like an adjective.
You don't need to work all this out alone: every word in the app has its label. But knowing what the pieces are lets you see why the English is what it is.

entries.title: Present
match: present=an action seen as going on: present
entries.short: The verb form for an action seen as going on or repeated. In a statement it usually means now: λύω, “I loose” (set free) or “I am loosing”.

body.p: The present views an action from the inside, as it unfolds, or as something that happens again and again. In statements it usually refers to now: λέγει, “he says”, or “he is saying”. In commands it often means “keep doing”: see [[imperative]].

Greek storytellers, especially Mark and John, sometimes switch into the present in the middle of a past story to make it vivid: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς, “and he says to them”. Grammar books call this the historic present, and [[translations|English translations]] usually turn it back into the past.

entries.title: Imperfect
match: imperfect=an action going on in the past: “was doing”
entries.short: An action going on, repeated or begun in the past: “he was teaching”, “he used to teach”, “he began to teach”.

body.p: The imperfect takes the [[present]]'s view of an action (from the inside, as ongoing) and sets it in the past. It is made from the present stem with an [[augment]] at the front: ἐδίδασκεν, “he was teaching”, from διδάσκω.

English can translate it in several ways depending on the context: “he was teaching”, “he kept teaching”, “he used to teach” or “he began to teach”. In stories, the imperfect often paints the background while the [[aorist]] tells the main events.
Hebrew grammar uses the same word, imperfect, for a quite different form: see [[imperfect-hebrew]].

entries.title: Future
match: future=an action still to come
2nd future=a future built on a different stem, most often a passive future without θ
entries.short: The form for what will happen: σώσει, “he will save”. It usually adds σ to the stem.

body.p: The Greek future is the one form that is mainly about time. It is usually made by adding σ before the ending: σώσει, “he will save”, from σῴζω. Sometimes the σ hides inside another letter: ὄψεσθε, “you will see”, has it in ψ (π + σ). When the stem ends in a consonant, the σ combines with it: ἄξω, from ἄγω. Some verbs form their future from a different stem, and STEPBible labels some of these “2nd future”: see [[second-aorist|“2nd” forms]].
The future can also give a solemn command, especially in quotations from the Old Testament: οὐ φονεύσεις, “you shall not murder”.

entries.title: Aorist
match: aorist=an action seen as a whole event
entries.short: The form that presents an action simply, as a whole event. In a statement it usually means the past: ἐπίστευσεν, “he believed”.

body.p: The aorist is the most common past form in Greek stories. It views an action from outside, as a single whole, without saying whether it took a moment or a long time. “Jesus wept”, ἐδάκρυσεν, is aorist.

In the [[indicative]] the aorist has an [[augment]] and usually means the past. In the other moods it has no augment and says nothing about time: an aorist [[imperative]] or [[subjunctive]] simply presents the action as a whole: πίστευσον, “believe!”.

The word comes from Greek ἀόριστος, “without limits”: the form leaves open how the action unfolded. It is not a special “once for all” [[tense]], though a writer may of course describe a once-for-all event with it.
Most aorists add σα to the stem: ἔλυσα, “I loosed”. Many common verbs form it differently, without the σ: see [[second-aorist]].

entries.title: 2nd aorist (and other “2nd” forms)
match: 2nd aorist=an aorist formed from a different stem, without σ
2nd perfect=a perfect formed without the usual κ
2nd pluperfect=a pluperfect formed without the usual κ
entries.short: An [[aorist]] made in an older way, from a changed stem and without σ: ἔλαβον, “I took”, from λαμβάνω. It means exactly the same as any aorist.

body.p: The “2nd” is about how the form is made, not what it means. Some of the commonest verbs have a 2nd aorist: ἔρχομαι, “I come”, has ἦλθον, “I came”; λαμβάνω has ἔλαβον; βάλλω has ἔβαλον; and λέγω has εἶπον, “I said”.

In the [[indicative]] these forms have the [[augment]], but instead of -σα- they put the endings of the [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]] on a different stem. So ἔβαλλον (imperfect, “I was throwing”) and ἔβαλον (2nd aorist, “I threw”) differ by one letter. This is why dictionaries list the main forms of each verb: see [[principal-parts]].

STEPBible's labels also mark “2nd perfect”, “2nd pluperfect” and “2nd future” for the same reason: forms made without the usual sign (κ for the [[perfect-greek|perfect]]; for the future, usually θ in the passive). Under each word the app shortens all of these to plain “aor.”, “perf.” and so on, because the meaning is the same.

entries.title: Perfect
match: perfect=a finished action whose result still stands
entries.short: The form for a finished action whose result still stands: γέγραπται, “it is written” (it was written and stands written).

body.p: The perfect looks back at a completed action from the state it has left. τετέλεσται, “it is finished” ([JHN 19:30]), means the work has been completed and stays completed. γέγραπται, “it is written”, introduces a scripture that was written and still stands.

Most perfects start with [[reduplication]], a doubling of the first sound with ε: λέλυκα, “I have loosed”, πεπίστευκα, “I have believed”. Many add κ before the ending. English often translates the perfect with “has” or “have”, but sometimes with a plain present: οἶδα, a perfect in form, means “I know”.

entries.title: Pluperfect
match: pluperfect=a finished action whose result stood at a past time
entries.short: The past of the [[perfect-greek|perfect]]: a result that stood at some time in the past: “he had come”, “it had been founded”.

body.p: The pluperfect is rare. It sets the state of a [[perfect-greek|perfect]] in the past: “the house did not fall, for it *had been founded* on the rock” ([MAT 7:25]). It usually has [[reduplication]], and sometimes an [[augment]] as well. Its active endings have ει in them: ᾔδει, “he knew” ([MRK 9:6]); the passive τεθεμελίωτο doesn't.

entries.title: Augment: the mark of the past
entries.short: An ε added to the front of a verb, or a lengthened first vowel, that marks past time in the [[indicative]]: λύω, ἔλυον, “I was loosing”.

body.p: The augment is a sign of the past, and only in the indicative: the [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]], [[aorist]] and [[pluperfect]]. When a verb begins with a consonant, ε is added: βλέπω, ἔβλεψα, “I saw”. When it begins with a vowel, that vowel is lengthened instead: ἀκούω, ἤκουσα, “I heard”; ἐγείρω, “I raise”, ἤγειρα, “I raised”.
With verbs that have a [[preposition]] at the front, the augment goes after it, between it and the verb: ἐκβάλλω, ἐξέβαλεν, “he drove out”. Finding the augment helps you find the stem to look up.

entries.title: Reduplication
entries.short: Doubling the first consonant of a verb with ε, the mark of the [[perfect-greek|perfect]]: λύω, λέλυκα, “I have loosed”.

body.p: Reduplication means “doubling again”. To make the [[perfect-greek|perfect]], Greek repeats the verb's first consonant with ε in front of the stem: πιστεύω, πεπίστευκα; γράφω, γέγραφα. When the verb starts with a vowel, the vowel is lengthened instead, as with the [[augment]].
Unlike the augment, reduplication stays in every mood, so it marks a perfect wherever it appears, including in [[participle|participles]]: ὁ γεγεννημένος, “the one who has been born”.

entries.title: Middle
match: middle=the subject acts for itself, or is involved in the action
middle deponent=middle in form, often active in meaning
entries.short: The voice in which the subject is involved in its own action, often doing it for itself or to itself: ἐνίψατο, “he washed (himself)”.

body.p: English has active (“I wash”) and passive (“I am washed”). Greek also has the middle, which says the subject is involved in the action in a closer way than usual: doing it for itself, to itself, or with its own interests in view. ἐνίψατο, “he washed himself” or “he washed his own (hands)”. Others have it simply as their way of saying something: ἀπεκρίνατο, “he answered”.

Often the difference is hard to bring into English, and many verbs simply have their meaning in the middle form: ἔρχομαι, “I come”, γίνομαι, “I become”, πορεύομαι, “I go”. These are the verbs older grammars call [[deponent]].

entries.title: Middle or passive
match: middle or passive=one form serving for both middle and passive
middle or passive deponent=one form for both voices, often active in meaning
entries.short: A form that could be either middle or passive, because in four tenses the two voices share their endings.

body.p: In the [[present]], [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]], [[perfect-greek|perfect]] and [[pluperfect]], the [[middle]] and [[passive]] endings are identical: λύομαι can be “I loose (for myself)” or “I am loosed”. Only the context shows which. STEPBible's labels say “middle or passive” where they have not chosen between them, and the app shortens it to “mid./pass.”.
In the [[aorist]] and [[future]], the passive has its own endings, usually with θη in them: ἐλύθη, “it was set free”.

entries.title: Deponent
match: deponent=middle or passive in form, active in meaning
passive deponent=passive in form, often active in meaning
entries.short: A verb with [[middle-or-passive|middle or passive]] endings but an active meaning, such as ἔρχομαι, “I come”. Many scholars now prefer to call these middle verbs.

body.p: ἔρχομαι, “I come”, has the endings of the [[middle]] or [[passive]], but it has no passive meaning (“I am being come” makes no sense). Older grammars said such verbs had “laid aside” (Latin *deponere*) their active forms, and called them deponent. STEPBible's labels use that word: “middle deponent”, “passive deponent”, “middle or passive deponent”.

Many scholars today think the label is misleading. These verbs mostly describe things in which the subject is closely involved: coming and going, becoming, feeling, thinking, receiving. That is just what the middle voice expresses, so they are simply middle verbs. For reading, the point is the same either way: translate them as active.

entries.title: Subjunctive
match: subjunctive=what may or should happen: possibility, purpose, “let us”
entries.short: The form of a verb for what may or should happen, rather than what does: after “so that”, “if”, “whoever”, and for “let us…”.

body.p: The subjunctive is recognised by ω or η in its ending where the ordinary form has ο or ε: λύωμεν, “let us set free”, compared with λύομεν, “we set free”. It has no [[augment]], and in the subjunctive the [[aorist]] and [[present]] differ only in [[aspect]], not in time.
Its main uses:

ul: purpose, after ἵνα, “so that”: ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων… μὴ ἀπόληται, “so that everyone who believes… should not perish” ([JHN 3:16]);
conditions and “whoever” [[sentence-parts|clauses]] with ἐάν or ἄν: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν, “if we confess”;
“let us”, in the 1st person plural: ἄγωμεν, “let us go”;
“do not”, with μή and the aorist: see [[prohibition]];
the strongest “never”, οὐ μή: “he will never die”.

entries.title: Optative
match: optative=a wish or a remote possibility: “may it be”
entries.short: A rare form for wishes and remote possibilities: μὴ γένοιτο, “may it never be!”.

body.p: The optative was dying out in New Testament times, and appears only rarely. Its endings usually have ι after the vowel: οι, αι or ει (γένοιτο, “may it be”; εἴη, “might be”). Paul's famous μὴ γένοιτο, “by no means!”, literally “may it not happen”, is an optative. Luke also uses it in polite or uncertain questions: “what this might be”.

entries.title: Greek infinitives
entries.short: The Greek “to” form of a verb: λύειν, “to set free”. It ends in -ειν, -σαι, -ναι or -σθαι, and is often used where English needs a whole clause.

body.p: The commonest endings of the [[infinitive]] are -ειν ([[present]] active, λύειν), -σαι ([[aorist]] active, λῦσαι), -ναι (εἶναι, “to be”) and -σθαι ([[middle]] or [[passive]], ἔρχεσθαι, “to come”). The infinitive has a [[tense]] and a [[voice]] but no [[person]].
Besides “to go” after verbs like “want” or “be able”, Greek uses the infinitive in many ways English doesn't:

ul: with “the” in front, as a noun: τὸ ζῆν Χριστός, “to live is Christ” ([PHP 1:21]);
after a preposition with “the”, for time or reason: ἐν τῷ σπείρειν, “while he was sowing”;
with its own subject in the [[accusative]]: “for him to go”, “that he goes”.

entries.title: Greek participles
entries.short: A Greek verb used like an adjective, with case endings. It can describe someone (“the one who believes”) or set the scene for the main verb (“having said this, he went out”).

body.p: A [[participle]] has the [[tense]] and [[voice]] of a verb and the [[case]], [[number]] and [[gender]] of an [[adjective]]. Its endings include -ων, -ουσα, -ον (present active), -σας ([[aorist]] active) and -μενος ([[middle-or-passive|middle or passive]]).
With “the” in front, a participle names a person by what they do: ὁ πιστεύων, “the one who believes”, or “whoever believes”. English usually needs a “who” clause.

Without “the”, a participle usually tells you something about the main action: when, why or how it happened. εἰπὼν ταῦτα ἐξῆλθεν, “having said this, he went out”, or “when he had said this…”. As a rule, a [[present]] participle happens at the same time as the main verb (“while…”), and an [[aorist]] participle before it (“after…”).
Greek writers often string several participles before one main verb, where English would use “and” several times.

entries.title: Genitive absolute
entries.short: A [[participle]] and its subject both in the [[genitive]], setting the scene: “while he was still speaking…”.

body.p: When a participle's own subject is not part of the main sentence, Greek puts both in the [[genitive]]: ἔτι αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος, “while he was still speaking” ([MAT 12:46]). The phrase stands apart from the rest of the sentence (“absolute” means “set free”), like a stage direction. Translate it with “while”, “when” or “after”.

entries.title: Contract verbs
entries.short: Verbs whose [[stem]] ends in α, ε or ο, which merges with the vowel of the ending: ποιέω, “I do”, is written ποιῶ.

body.p: Some verb stems end in a vowel: ποιε-, ἀγαπα-, δικαιο-. When an ending starting with a vowel is added, the two vowels merge (contract): ποιε- + -ει becomes ποιεῖ, “he does”; ἀγαπα- + -ει becomes ἀγαπᾷ, “he loves”; δικαιο- + -εται becomes δικαιοῦται, “he is justified”.

Dictionaries list these verbs in their uncontracted form, which rarely appears in the text: ποιέω, ἀγαπάω, δικαιόω. That way you can see the stem's vowel. A [[accents|circumflex accent]] (῀) on the ending is often a sign of contraction.

entries.title: The verb “to be”: εἰμί
entries.short: The commonest and most irregular Greek verb: εἰμί, “I am”, ἐστίν, “he is”, ἦν, “he was”. It is followed by the [[nominative]], not the [[accusative]].

body.p: εἰμί has its own set of forms that must simply be learned:

now

body.p: What follows “is” describes the [[subject]], so it is in the [[nominative]] too: ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν, “God is love”. Often ἐστίν is left out altogether, and English has to supply “is”: see [[verbless-clause]].
STEPBible's labels give εἰμί the voice “active”, as a convention: it has no passive. Its [[future]] has middle endings: ἔσομαι, “I will be”.

entries.title: Principal parts
entries.short: The handful of forms of a verb from which all its other forms are built. Learning them makes irregular verbs recognisable.

body.p: Every Greek verb has up to six main forms: the [[present]], [[future]], [[aorist]] active, [[perfect-greek|perfect]] active, perfect middle and aorist passive. All its other forms are built from one of these. For regular verbs they follow a pattern: πιστεύω, πιστεύσω, ἐπίστευσα, πεπίστευκα, πεπίστευμαι, ἐπιστεύθην. For irregular verbs they don't, which is why dictionaries list them: ὁράω, “I see”, has the aorist εἶδον and the future ὄψομαι.
A beginner doesn't need to learn whole lists. It helps to know that a strange-looking form may still be a common verb, and the app always shows the [[dictionary-form]].

entries.title: Sentences without “is”
entries.short: Greek and especially Hebrew often leave out “is” or “are”, and English adds it: “blessed the man”, meaning “blessed *is* the man”.

body.p: English needs a verb in every sentence. Greek can leave out ἐστίν: μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοί, literally “blessed the poor”, is “blessed *are* the poor”. Hebrew does this all the time, because it has no common word for “is” in the present: יְהוָה רֹעִי, literally “the LORD my shepherd”, is “the LORD *is* my shepherd” ([PSA 23:1]).
That is why English Bibles add “is” or “are”, sometimes printing it in italics. In the app, a word that English adds is shown in square brackets in the word-by-word English.

entries.title: The Hebrew alphabet
entries.short: Hebrew has twenty-two letters, all consonants, written from right to left. Five of them have a different shape at the end of a word.

body.p: The alphabet runs from א, aleph, to ת, tav. Every letter is a consonant: the vowels are shown by marks added around the letters ([[vowel-points]]). Two letters, א and ע, are silent in the app's pronunciation, and ו and י can also stand for vowels ([[matres]]).

Several letters look alike and are worth practising in pairs: ב and כ, ד and ר, ה and ח, ו and ז, ס and ם. The [[#/alphabet/he|Letters tab]] shows each letter with its name, its sound and words to hear.

entries.title: Final letters
entries.short: Five letters change shape at the end of a word: כ becomes ך, מ becomes ם, נ becomes ן, פ becomes ף, and צ becomes ץ. The sound stays the same.

body.p: The final shapes mostly reach down below the line, or close up. They only mark the end of a word: מֶלֶךְ, “king”, ends in ך; the plural מְלָכִים has the ordinary כ in the middle and ם at the end. When you search the [[words-tab|Words tab]], the app treats each letter and its final form as the same letter.

entries.title: Vowel points
entries.short: The dots and dashes under, over and beside Hebrew letters that show the vowels. They were added by the [[masoretes]]; the letters themselves are consonants.

body.p: Each vowel mark is said after the letter it is attached to: בָּ is “ba”, בִּ is “bi”. The vowels fall into three families:
Some vowels are written with a letter as well: וֹ (holam with ו) is o, וּ (shureq) is u, and ִי is i. See [[matres]]. There is also a mark for “no vowel” or a very short one: the [[shewa]].

The Masoretes added these marks to a text that was already centuries old, to record exactly how it was read. That is why one Hebrew word can have a dot inside a letter, a vowel under it and an accent too.

entries.title: Vowel letters: ה, ו and י
entries.short: The letters ה, ו and י sometimes stand for a vowel instead of a consonant: וֹ is o, וּ is u, ִי is i, and a final ה after a vowel is silent.

body.p: Before vowel marks existed, scribes used a few letters to hint at vowels, and they still do the job: in טוֹב, “good”, the ו is the vowel o; in דָּוִד, “David”, the ו is a consonant, v. A ה at the end of a word after a vowel is silent, as in תּוֹרָה, “law”, unless it has a dot ([[dagesh|mappiq]]).
The same word may be spelt with or without the vowel letter: לֹא and לוֹא are both “not”. Grammars call these full and short (or plene and defective) spellings. The meaning is the same.

entries.title: Dagesh: the dot inside a letter
entries.short: A dot inside a letter. In ב, כ and פ it makes the hard sound (b, k, p); after a vowel it doubles the letter: הַשָּׁמַיִם has a doubled שׁ.

body.p: The same dot does three jobs:

ul: in the six letters ב ג ד כ פ ת at the start of a word or after a consonant, it marks the hard sound: בּ is b, without the dot ב is v. This is the dagesh lene (“light”); see [[begadkefat]];

after a vowel, it doubles the letter: הַשָּׁמַיִם is hash-sha-MA-yim, “the heavens”. This is the dagesh forte (“strong”), and it often shows that something has been added, such as the article “the”, or that a letter has dropped out;
in a final ה it shows the ה is sounded, not silent: לָהּ, “to her”. This dot is called mappiq.

body.p: A small line over a letter, called rafe, marks that a letter has no dagesh. The Leningrad Codex uses it often, and the Reader shows it.

entries.title: The six letters with two sounds: ב ג ד כ פ ת
entries.short: Six letters, ב ג ד כ פ ת, have a hard sound with a dot inside (b, g, d, k, p, t) and a soft one without it. In the app's pronunciation only ב, כ and פ change: to v, kh and f.

body.p: The six are remembered by the made-up word begadkefat. With a [[dagesh]] they are hard: בּ b, כּ k, פּ p. Without it, after a vowel, they are soft: ב v, כ kh (as in Scottish “loch”), פ f. So the same root can be heard two ways: כָּתַב, ka-TAV, “he wrote”, and יִכְתֹּב, yikh-TOV, “he will write”.
In ancient times ג, ד and ת also had soft sounds (gh, th as in “this”, th as in “thin”). Modern pronunciation, and the app's, says them the same with or without the dot.

entries.title: Shewa: said and silent
entries.short: Two dots under a letter, one above the other (בְ). At the start of a syllable it is said as a very short e; at the end of one it is silent.

body.p: The shewa marks a letter with either a very short vowel or none at all. The rule of thumb: it is said (“vocal”) where it starts a [[syllables|syllable]], and silent where it closes one.

ul: At the start of a word it is said: בְּרִית, be-RIT, “covenant”.
After a short vowel, closing the syllable, it is silent: יִשְׁמֹר, yish-MOR.
Of two shewas in a row, the second is said: יִשְׁמְרוּ, yish-me-RU.
Under a doubled letter, it is said: הַמְּלָכִים, ham-me-la-KHIM.
After a long vowel, it is said: יָלְדָה, ya-le-DAH, “she bore”.

body.p: In everyday Israeli Hebrew many said shewas are dropped (brit instead of be-RIT). The app follows the academic pronunciation and says them, and its Hebrew voice is given a short e wherever the shewa is said. Under the [[gutturals|throat letters]], a said shewa is replaced by a [[hateph|hateph]] vowel.

entries.title: Hateph vowels: a quick a, e or o
entries.short: A [[shewa]] joined to another vowel makes a very quick a, e or o: אֲנִי, a-NI; אֱלֹהִים, e-lo-HIM; חֳלִי, cho-LI. They are used mostly under the [[gutturals|throat letters]], which can't take an ordinary said shewa.

body.p: Where another letter would have a said shewa, the throat letters א ה ח ע usually take a hateph (“hurried”) vowel instead: אֱלֹהִים, e-lo-HIM, “God”; אֲנִי, a-NI, “I”; חֳלִי, cho-LI, “sickness”. Say them like the full vowel, but quickly.

entries.title: Throat letters: א ה ח ע
entries.short: The four letters made in the throat, א ה ח ע. They never take the doubling dot, prefer a-vowels, and take a hateph vowel instead of a said [[shewa]]. ר behaves like them in some ways.

body.p: Because these letters are made at the back of the throat, Hebrew changes the vowels around them. They can't be doubled, so a vowel before them often lengthens instead: “the” is הָ in הָאָרֶץ, “the earth”, not הַ with a doubling dot. They like a-vowels, which is why a word such as נַעַר, “young man”, has a where מֶלֶךְ, “king”, has e. And they take [[hateph|hateph]] vowels instead of a said shewa.
ר is not made in the throat, but it also refuses the doubling dot. Most grammars count it among the gutturals for that reason; the app's lessons treat it on its own.

entries.title: Furtive patah
entries.short: A patah under a final ח, ע or הּ after another vowel is said before the letter, not after it: רוּחַ is RU-ach, “spirit”.

body.p: After a vowel such as u, o or e, it is hard to say a throat letter at the very end of a word. So Hebrew slips in a short a just before it: רוּחַ, RU-ach, not ru-CHA; גָּבֹהַּ, ga-VO-ah, “high”. The patah under the last letter is written there, but said before it. It is never stressed.

entries.title: Qamets hatuf: the qamets said o
entries.short: The mark ָ is usually a (qamets), but in a closed, unstressed syllable it is a short o: כָּל־ is kol, “all”; חָכְמָה is chokh-MAH, “wisdom”.

body.p: Hebrew uses one mark for two sounds. In most places ָ is a long a. But where it stands in a syllable that ends in a consonant and has no stress, it is a short o, called qamets hatuf: כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, kol ha-A-rets, “all the earth”. Some editions print the short o with a slightly longer stem (ׇ) to tell them apart, and some dictionary forms in the app use it.
The [[masoretes]] said their qamets like the o in British “law”, which is why one sign could cover both. The app's Hebrew voice gets the o wherever the spelling or the grammar settles it.

entries.title: Syllables and stress in Hebrew
entries.short: Most Hebrew words are stressed on the last syllable: da-VAR, “word”. Some, such as מֶלֶךְ, ME-lekh, are stressed on the one before.

body.p: A Hebrew syllable almost always starts with a consonant and has one vowel: בָּרָא, “he created”, is two syllables, ba and RA. A syllable that ends in a vowel is open; one that ends in a consonant is closed.

Most words are stressed on the last syllable. A large group of nouns, called segolates because many have two segols, are stressed on the one before: מֶלֶךְ, ME-lekh, “king”; אֶרֶץ, E-rets, “land”; נַעַר, NA-ar, “young man” (a, not e, because of the [[gutturals|throat letter]] ע). Some verb endings are unstressed too. Grammars call stress on the last syllable milra and stress on the one before milel, from Aramaic words for “below” and “above”.
The [[cantillation|accent marks]] show which syllable is stressed. In the app's respellings the stressed syllable is in capitals.

entries.title: Stress: the strong syllable
entries.short: The syllable said a little louder and longer than the others: the first syllable of “TA-ble”, the second of “a-GO”. The app writes it in capitals.

body.p: In English, putting the stress in the wrong place can change a word (“RE-cord” and “re-CORD”). In Greek and Hebrew it matters too, and the texts show it. In Greek the [[accents]] mark the stressed syllable. In Hebrew most words carry an accent mark on the stressed syllable ([[cantillation]]), and the stress usually falls on the last syllable ([[syllables]]).

The app's [[respelling|respellings]] write the stressed syllable in capitals: λόγος LO-gos, דָּבָר da-VAR. The Hebrew voice on your phone chooses its own stress, so it may sometimes stress a word differently from the respelling.

entries.title: Maqqef: the joining line
entries.short: A short line at the top of the letters (־) that joins two words to be said as one, with one stress: כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, kol ha-A-rets, “all the earth”.

body.p: The maqqef works like a hyphen. Words joined by it are read together, and the first word loses its own stress, which can change its vowel: כֹּל, “all”, becomes כָּל־ (kol, with a short o, see [[qamets-hatuf]]). It often joins short words such as כָּל־, אֶת־ and עַל־ to the next word, and links nouns in a [[construct-state|construct]] chain. The Reader shows maqqef-joined words with no space between them.

entries.title: Accent marks (cantillation)
entries.short: Small marks above and below Hebrew words that show the stressed syllable, how the words of a verse group together, and the tune for chanting it aloud.

body.p: Almost every word in the Hebrew Bible has one of about thirty accent marks. They do three jobs at once. They show the stressed syllable, because most sit on it. They work as punctuation: some divide the verse (disjunctive accents, like commas and semicolons) and others join a word to the next (conjunctive accents). And they are a musical notation for chanting the text in the synagogue.

You don't need to learn them all. The most useful are the two strongest dividers: atnah (ב֑), under the word that ends the first half of a verse, and silluq (בֽ), on the last word, before the [[sof-pasuq]]. The app's Hebrew voice pauses at both. The [[letters-tab|Letters tab]] shows how they look.

entries.title: Meteg
entries.short: A small upright line beside a vowel (בָֽ) that slows the syllable down. It can show that a qamets is a long a, not an o.

body.p: The meteg (“bridle”) marks a syllable that should not be rushed, often two syllables before the stress: הָֽאָדָם, ha-a-DAM, “the man”. Because a long a is said slowly and a short o is not, a meteg beside a qamets is usually a clue that it is a long a: שָֽׁמְרוּ is sha-me-RU, “they kept”. Commands are the exception: in שָֽׁמְרֵנִי, “keep me” ([PSA 16:1]), the qamets is a short o said slowly, sho-me-RE-ni. It looks exactly like silluq ([[cantillation]]), which only comes on the last word of a verse.

entries.title: Sof pasuq: the end of a verse
entries.short: Two dots like a colon (׃) at the end of every verse in the Hebrew Bible. Its name means “end of verse”.

body.p: It works like a full stop at the end of the verse. The last word before it also carries silluq, the strongest of the [[cantillation|accent marks]]. The Reader keeps it, and the Hebrew voice stops there.

entries.title: Paseq: a small upright line
entries.short: A thin upright line between two words (׀). It keeps them apart in reading, a little like a slight pause.

body.p: The paseq (“divider”) stands between words that should not run together, sometimes to avoid slurring two similar sounds, sometimes for emphasis, and it also forms part of some accents. It is rare and doesn't change the meaning. The Reader shows it with a space on each side.

entries.title: פ and ס: paragraph marks
entries.short: A פ or a ס standing on its own between verses marks the end of a paragraph. They are not words, and the app uses them to start a new paragraph.

body.p: The scribes divided the text into sections with gaps on the page: an open section (פְּתוּחָה, petuha) started on a new line, and a closed one (סְתוּמָה, setuma) after a space in the same line. Printed Bibles show these gaps with a single letter, פ or ס. They are older than the chapter and [[verse-numbers|verse numbers]].
The app doesn't print or say these letters. In the running-text layout it starts a new paragraph where they stand.

entries.title: Ketiv and qere: written one way, read another
entries.short: In over a thousand places the [[masoretes]] noted that a word is written one way (ketiv) but read another (qere). The app shows the read form, marked °, and gives the written form when you tap it.

body.p: The Masoretes would not change a letter of the text they had received, even where it seemed wrong or where the tradition read it differently. Instead they wrote the vowels of the word to be read (the qere, “what is read”) under the letters as written (the ketiv, “what is written”), and noted the reading in the margin.

The app's text shows the qere, the word as it is read aloud, with a small ° after it. Tap the word, and the word sheet shows the ketiv under “Written”. In the Hebrew text the app uses, {{qere}} words are marked this way.
The most frequent case is never marked at all: God's name, see [[divine-name]].

entries.title: The name of God: יהוה
entries.short: God's name, written with four letters, יהוה. By long Jewish custom it is not said aloud: readers say Adonai, “my Lord”, which is why English Bibles print LORD.

body.p: The four letters יהוה (Y-H-W-H) are the personal name of God, used thousands of times in the Old Testament. Out of reverence, Jewish readers had stopped saying it aloud by the time of Jesus, and read אֲדֹנָי, Adonai, “my Lord”, instead. The New Testament and most copies of the [[septuagint]] likewise write κύριος, “Lord”, though a few early Septuagint copies keep the four Hebrew letters.

The [[masoretes]] wrote יהוה with vowels taken from Adonai, as a permanent [[ketiv-qere|qere]], so that nobody would say the name. The form “Jehovah” came about when later Christian readers combined those vowels with the letters. Scholars think the name was originally said something like Yahweh.

English Bibles follow the reading custom by printing LORD in small capitals. Where Adonai and יהוה stand together, the name is written with the vowels of אֱלֹהִים, Elohim, “God”, and read Elohim, so English prints “Lord GOD”. The app's Hebrew voice says Adonai or Elohim in the same way.

entries.title: Written but not read
entries.short: A few words are written in the Hebrew text but, by long tradition, not read aloud. The Reader shows them in grey, and the voice leaves them out.

body.p: In a handful of places the [[masoretes]] marked a word to be skipped when reading aloud, usually because it seemed to be written twice or to belong elsewhere. They kept it in the text, without its own vowels for reading. The app shows such words in grey and explains them when tapped. There are {{notread}} of them in the Hebrew text the app uses.

entries.title: Words supplied from other manuscripts
entries.short: A few words missing from the Leningrad Codex are added from other manuscripts or old translations. The Reader shows them in square brackets.

body.p: Every manuscript has its faults. Where the Leningrad Codex seems to have lost a word or phrase that other Hebrew manuscripts, the Samaritan Pentateuch or early translations such as the [[septuagint]] have, STEPBible supplies it and marks it. The app shows these words in [square brackets] and explains them when tapped. A well-known example is [GEN 4:8], where Cain's words to Abel, “let us go out to the field”, are missing from the Hebrew.

entries.title: Extraordinary dots over letters
entries.short: In fifteen places, ancient scribes put dots over certain letters or words, probably to mark them as doubtful. The app shows them, but they don't change how the word is read.

body.p: The dots are older than the vowel marks, and their meaning was already debated in ancient times. Most likely they marked letters the scribes doubted but would not remove. One example is the dots over וְאַהֲרֹן, “and Aaron”, in [NUM 3:39]. The app ignores them when reading aloud.

entries.title: Inverted nun: ׆
entries.short: A reversed letter נ (׆) that stands in a few places, such as around [NUM 10:35] and [NUM 10:36]. It seems to mark a passage as set apart. It is not read.

body.p: The inverted nun appears around the “Song of the Ark” in Numbers and several times in [PSA 107:23|Psalm 107]. The ancient rabbis already discussed why: perhaps the passage stood somewhere else, or formed a book on its own. The app shows the sign and doesn't read it aloud.

entries.title: Psalm titles
entries.short: Many psalms begin with a title, such as “A Psalm of David”. Hebrew Bibles number it as part of the verses; English Bibles don't number it. The Reader shows it as “title”.

body.p: The titles name an author, an occasion, a tune or a musical direction, and they are part of the Hebrew text. In Hebrew Bibles a short title shares verse one with the psalm's first line, so the numbers agree with English Bibles. A longer title is verse one on its own, or even verses one and two ([PSA 51:1|Psalm 51]), and then the psalm's verses are numbered one or two higher than in English Bibles. The app follows English numbering, shows the title at the start labelled “title”, and puts the Hebrew number beside each verse where it differs: see [[verse-numbers]].

entries.title: Root
entries.short: The consonants, usually three, that carry a family of related meanings: מ־ל־ך is behind מֶלֶךְ, “king”, and מָלַךְ, “he reigned”.

body.p: Most Hebrew words are built on a root of three consonants. The vowels and the letters added before, after or inside the root make different words from it, all with related meanings. From the root מ־ל־ך come מֶלֶךְ, “king”, מָלַךְ, “he reigned”, מַלְכָּה, “queen”, and מַמְלָכָה, “kingdom”.

Recognising the root is the main skill in reading Hebrew. Once you can find the three letters underneath, you can often guess the meaning of a word you have never seen, and you know where to look it up. Some roots have a weak letter that drops out or changes in some forms (often א, ה, ו, י or נ), which makes them harder to spot: see [[weak-verbs]].

entries.title: Hebrew nouns: gender, number and endings
entries.short: A Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine, and singular, plural or [[dual]]. Plurals usually end in -ִים (masculine) or -וֹת (feminine).

body.p: Most masculine nouns have no special ending in the singular, and add -ִים in the plural: סוּס, “horse”, סוּסִים, “horses”. Most feminine nouns end in -ָה or -ת, and their plural ends in -וֹת: מִצְוָה, “commandment”, מִצְוֹת, “commandments”.

There are exceptions, and the [[gender]] of the noun doesn't always match its plural ending: אָבוֹת, “fathers”, is masculine. As in Greek, the gender is a matter of grammar, but it decides the form of adjectives and verbs that go with the noun.

Hebrew nouns don't have [[case]] endings as Greek ones do. Instead, a noun's form changes when it is joined to the noun after it ([[construct-state]]), and when it takes an ending such as “my” or “his” ([[pronoun-suffix]]).

entries.title: The dual: two of something
match: dual=two, a pair
entries.short: A Hebrew noun form for two of something, ending -ַיִם: יָדַיִם, “two hands”. It is used mostly for things that come in pairs.

body.p: Hebrew has a special ending, -ַיִם, for two of something. It is used for pairs of body parts, such as עֵינַיִם, “eyes”, and רַגְלַיִם, “feet”, and for a few words of time and number: יוֹמַיִם, “two days”, שְׁנַיִם, “two”. Things that come in pairs keep the dual even when there are more than two: the seraphim each had שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם, “six wings” ([ISA 6:2]).
Two common words only look dual and are really ordinary words: שָׁמַיִם, “heaven”, and מַיִם, “water”.

entries.title: Absolute state
match: absolute=the ordinary form of a noun, standing on its own
entries.short: The ordinary form of a Hebrew noun, standing on its own: דָּבָר, “word”. Its partner is the construct form, joined to the next word.

body.p: A Hebrew noun has two kinds of form. The absolute is the noun on its own, as in a dictionary: דָּבָר, “a word”, הַדָּבָר, “the word”. The [[construct-state]] is the form used when it is joined to the noun after it in an “of” phrase: דְּבַר, “word of”. STEPBible's labels say which one each noun is.

entries.title: Construct state: “of” in Hebrew
match: construct=joined to the next word: “… of”
entries.short: A Hebrew noun joined to the noun after it to mean “… of …”: דְּבַר יְהוָה, “the word of the LORD”. The first noun is in its construct form.

body.p: Hebrew has no word for “of”. It puts two nouns side by side, and the first one changes its form slightly, often shortening its vowels, to show it belongs to the second: דָּבָר, “word”, becomes דְּבַר in דְּבַר יְהוָה, “the word of the LORD”. This joined form is the construct. Two or more nouns joined this way are called a construct chain, and are often linked by a [[maqqef]].

Two rules help. The first noun never takes “the”. And the whole phrase counts as “the” if the last noun has “the” or is a name: בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ is “*the* house of the king”, though בֵּית has no article.

The construct is used for the same kinds of meaning as the Greek [[genitive]]: belonging, source, material, and description, as in הַר קָדְשִׁי, “my holy mountain”, literally “the mountain of my holiness”.

entries.title: The Hebrew article: הַ
match: definite=with “the” built in
entries.short: Hebrew “the” is a prefix, הַ, joined to the front of a word, usually with a dot doubling the next letter: הַשָּׁמַיִם, “the heavens”.

body.p: The article is ה with a patah, and a [[dagesh]] that doubles the first letter of the word: מֶלֶךְ, “king”, הַמֶּלֶךְ, “the king”. Before the [[gutturals|throat letters]] and ר, which can't be doubled, the vowel changes instead. Before א, ע and ר it usually becomes הָ: הָאָרֶץ, “the earth”, הָעָם, “the people”. Before ה and ח it usually stays הַ, without the dot: הַחֹשֶׁךְ, “the darkness”. And before a ח with a qamets it becomes הֶ: הֶחָכָם, “the wise man”.

After the one-letter prepositions ב, כ and ל, the ה drops out and its vowel moves under the preposition: לַמֶּלֶךְ, “to the king”, instead of לְהַמֶּלֶךְ. STEPBible labels such a word “Preposition (definite)”.
Hebrew has no word for “a”. A noun without the article is indefinite, unless it is a name, has a “my”-type ending, or is joined to a definite noun ([[construct-state]]).

entries.title: One-letter prefixes
aka: ו ב כ ל מ ה ש
entries.short: Several short Hebrew words are written as one letter joined to the front of the next word: וְ “and”, בְּ “in”, כְּ “like”, לְ “to”, מִ “from”, הַ “the”.

body.p: Hebrew writes some of its commonest words as a single letter with a vowel, joined to the word after them. A word in the Bible can carry two or three of them: וּבַיּוֹם, “and on the day”, is “and” + “on” + “the” + “day”.

ul: וְ, “and”: see [[conjunction-vav]];
בְּ, “in”, “with”, “by”; כְּ, “like”, “as”; לְ, “to”, “for”: see [[hebrew-prepositions]];
מִ, “from”, a short form of מִן;
הַ, “the”: see [[hebrew-article]];
הֲ, which turns a sentence into a question: see [[interrogative-particle]];
שֶׁ, “who”, “which”: see [[hebrew-relative]].

body.p: When you tap a word in the Reader, “Word parts” shows each prefix and ending separately, with its meaning.

entries.title: וְ: “and”
match: consecutive conjunction=the “and” of a narrative verb (wayyiqtol)
entries.short: The letter ו joined to the front of a word means “and”, “but”, “so” or “then”. It is the commonest word in the Hebrew Bible.

body.p: The letter ו is called vav (grammars also spell it waw). As “and”, וְ is written as part of the next word. Its vowel changes with the sound after it: וּ before ב, מ or פ, or before a [[shewa]] (וּמֶלֶךְ, “and a king”); and in a few other places וַ or וָ.
Hebrew stories join almost every sentence with “and”, which is why older English Bibles start so many verses with “And”. Modern translations often use “then”, “so”, “but” or nothing at all.

A special form, וַ with a doubled letter after it, joins the [[wayyiqtol|narrative past]] form: וַיֹּאמֶר, “and he said”. STEPBible's labels call it the “consecutive conjunction”, and the app shows it as “and (narrative)”: see the entry on the wayyiqtol.

entries.title: Hebrew prepositions
entries.short: Three common Hebrew prepositions are one letter joined to the next word: בְּ “in”, כְּ “like”, לְ “to”. Others are separate words: מִן “from”, עַל “on”, אֶל “to”.

body.p: The one-letter prepositions are written with a [[shewa]] (בְּ, כְּ, לְ), and their vowel changes with the word after them: לֵאלֹהִים, “to God”, בַּשָּׁמַיִם, “in the heavens”, where the vowel shows the article was there (see [[hebrew-article]]).
מִן, “from”, can be a separate word, or shortened to מִ with a doubled letter after it: מִמִּצְרַיִם, “from Egypt”. It also makes comparisons: “good from” means “better than” (see [[comparative]]).
Prepositions can take [[pronoun-suffix|pronoun endings]]: לוֹ, “to him”, בָּהּ, “in her”, מִמֶּנּוּ, “from him”. See [[pronoun-suffix]].

entries.title: Pronoun endings: “my”, “his”, “them”
match: suffix=an ending for “my”, “his”, “them” and so on
entries.short: A short ending that means “my”, “your”, “his”, “her”, “our” or “their” on a noun, and “me”, “him”, “them” on a verb or preposition: דְּבָרוֹ, “his word”.

body.p: Instead of separate words for “my” and “his”, Hebrew adds an ending to the word:

On a verb the ending is the object: שָׁמְרֵנִי, “keep me”. On a preposition it is what the preposition governs: לָהֶם, “to them”. With a plural noun the endings change slightly: דְּבָרָיו, “his words”.
In the Reader, these endings are listed under “Word parts” as a suffix, with a label such as “suffix 3ms”, which means “his” or “him”: see [[pgn]].

entries.title: ה of direction: “towards”
match: directional suffix=the ending ה, “towards”
directional=towards
entries.short: An unstressed -ָה at the end of a place word, meaning “towards” or “to”: אַרְצָה, “to the land”, הַשָּׁמַיְמָה, “towards the heavens”.

body.p: Hebrew can show direction with an ending instead of a preposition. It is the vowel and ה, -ָה, added to a word for a place or a direction: מִצְרַיְמָה, “to Egypt”, צָפוֹנָה, “northwards”. Unlike the feminine ending -ָה, it is never stressed. The app shows it as “towards (ending)”.

entries.title: Added endings: paragogic hé and nun
match: paragogic hé=an extra ה on the end of a word
paragogic nun=an extra נ on the end of a verb
paragogic=added on the end
entries.short: An extra ה or נ added to the end of a word, often for emphasis or the rhythm of the sentence, without changing the basic meaning.

body.p: “Paragogic” means “added on”. Hebrew sometimes adds -ָה to a verb, especially to “let me” or “let us” forms ([[cohortative]]) and to commands: שִׁמְעָה, “hear!”. And it sometimes adds -וּן to a plural verb: יִשְׁמְעוּן, “they will hear”. Grammar books describe these as giving some emphasis or a fuller sound. STEPBible's labels show them with “!”, and the app calls them an “added ending”.

entries.title: אֵת: the object marker
match: object indicator=the small word אֵת, marking the object
entries.short: The small word אֵת (or אֶת־) marks the direct object of a verb when it is a particular, known person or thing. It has no English translation.

body.p: In [GEN 1:1], “God created *the heavens* and *the earth*”, the two objects each have אֵת in front of them: אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ. It shows which noun is the [[object]], since Hebrew word order is freer than English. It is used only when the object is definite: a name, a noun with “the”, or a noun with a “my”-type ending.
The app's English shows it as <obj.>, meaning “here is the object”, and leaves it untranslated. Don't confuse it with a different word, אֵת meaning “with”: the context decides.

entries.title: People groups: gentilic nouns
match: gentilic=a word for a member of a people, such as “Israelite”
people=a people group
entries.short: A word for a member of a people or a place: עִבְרִי, “Hebrew”, יְהוּדִי, “Jew”, Γαλιλαῖος, “Galilean”.

body.p: These words are made from the name of a people or place, as English makes “Israelite” from “Israel”. In Hebrew they usually end in -ִי: מִצְרִי, “Egyptian”. STEPBible calls them gentilic (from Latin *gens*, “people”), and the app shows them as “(people group)”.

entries.title: Hebrew pronouns: אֲנִי, אַתָּה, הוּא
entries.short: Separate Hebrew words for “I”, “you”, “he”, “she”, “we” and “they”, used mostly as the subject, often in sentences without a verb: אֲנִי יְהוָה, “I am the LORD”.

body.p: A Hebrew verb already shows who does the action, so these words are used for emphasis, or in [[verbless-clause|sentences without a verb]], where they act like “is”: אֲנִי יְהוָה, “I [am] the LORD”. For “me”, “my”, “him” and “his”, Hebrew uses [[pronoun-suffix|endings]] instead.

entries.title: אֲשֶׁר: “who”, “which”, “that”
match: relative particle=the word אֲשֶׁר, “who”, “which”, “that”
relative=the word אֲשֶׁר, “who”, “which”, “that”
entries.short: The Hebrew word that joins a clause to a noun: “the land *which* I will show you”. It never changes its form.

body.p: Unlike Greek [[relative|ὅς]], אֲשֶׁר has no endings. Hebrew often adds a pronoun later in the clause to show how it fits: “the land which you are lying on it” means “the land on which you are lying”. English leaves that extra word out.
A short form, שֶׁ, is joined to the next word, mostly in poetry and later books, such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.

entries.title: Question markers
match: interrogative particle=a word that turns a sentence into a question
entries.short: A word that turns a sentence into a question. In Hebrew it is the prefix הֲ: הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, “Am I my brother's keeper?”.

body.p: Hebrew writes no question mark. A question is shown by a question word such as מִי, “who?”, or by the prefix הֲ on the first word of a yes-or-no question. Don't confuse הֲ with the article הַ: the vowel is usually different, and the question הֲ doesn't double the next letter. Before a [[shewa]] or a [[gutturals|throat letter]] it is written הַ, and then only the missing dot tells them apart.
Greek has question particles too, and STEPBible labels them the same way, but a Greek question is usually shown by the question mark ; at the end (see [[greek-punctuation]]).

entries.title: זֶה, זֹאת, אֵלֶּה: “this”, “these”
match: demonstrative particle=“this” or “these”: a pointing word
entries.short: The Hebrew words for “this” and “these”: זֶה (masculine), זֹאת (feminine) and אֵלֶּה (plural). STEPBible labels them “demonstrative particle”.

body.p: They point to someone or something near, or just mentioned. After a noun with “the”, they take “the” too, and mean “this”: הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, “this day”, literally “the day, the this”. On their own they mean “this is” or “these are”: אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים, “these are the words”.
For “that” and “those”, Hebrew uses the words for “he”, “she” and “they”: הַיּוֹם הַהוּא, “that day”. The app's short label for these words is “this/that”.

entries.title: הִנֵּה: “look!”
entries.short: הִנֵּה, “look!”, “here is”, “behold”, draws attention to what follows. STEPBible labels it an interjection.

body.p: Older English Bibles translate it “behold”. Modern ones use “look”, “see”, “here is”, or show its sense with a word such as “suddenly” or “now”. It can take a pronoun ending: הִנֵּנִי, “here I am”, is Abraham's and Samuel's answer when God calls ([GEN 22:1], [1SA 3:4]), and Isaiah's answer is הִנְנִי ([ISA 6:8]).

entries.title: כִּי and אִם: “if”, “for”, “that”
match: conditional particle=a word such as כִּי or אִם: “if”, “for”, “that”
entries.short: Two very common Hebrew words. כִּי means “for”, “because”, “that” or “when”; אִם means “if”. STEPBible labels both “conditional particle”.

body.p: כִּי is one of the most used words in the Hebrew Bible, and its meaning depends on its place: “for” or “because” giving a reason, “that” after verbs of seeing and knowing, “when”, or “surely”. אִם means “if”, or “whether”, and in oaths it can mean “surely not”. כִּי אִם together often means “but rather” or “except”. STEPBible gives the same label to a few other joining words, such as לְמַעַן, “so that”, and פֶּן, “so that not”.
The app shows both as “conj. (if/for)” under the word.

entries.title: How a Hebrew verb is built
entries.short: A Hebrew verb is its root, shaped by a stem pattern, in one of a few forms, with prefixes or endings that show the person: וַיֹּאמֶר, “and he said”.

body.p: A grammar label for a Hebrew verb reads like this: “Verb: Qal (simple, active) consecutive imperfect (past/present indicative) third singular masculine”. Taking it in order:

ul: the stem, here [[qal]], with STEPBible's short description of it in brackets: see [[stems]];
the form, here the “consecutive imperfect”, better known as the [[wayyiqtol]], with a note on its usual time: see [[time-in-labels|how labels show time]];
the [[person]], [[number]] and [[gender]]: “he”. The app shortens this to 3ms: see [[pgn]].

body.p: The main forms are a handful. The [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] (qatal) uses endings: שָׁמַרְתִּי, “I kept”. The [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] (yiqtol) uses prefixes and sometimes endings: יִשְׁמֹר, “he will keep”. Joined to “and”, each of these has a narrative use: see [[wayyiqtol]] and [[weqatal]]. There are also commands ([[imperative]], [[jussive]], [[cohortative]]), two infinitives ([[infinitive-construct]], [[infinitive-absolute]]) and the [[hebrew-participle|participle]].

entries.title: Word order in Hebrew
entries.short: In a Hebrew story the verb usually comes first, then the subject, then the rest: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים, “and God said”, is literally “and said God”.

body.p: English puts the subject first: “God said”. Hebrew prose usually starts with the verb, especially the [[wayyiqtol]]: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר, “And God said, ‘Let there be light’” ([GEN 1:3]), word for word “and said God, let there be light”. The [[object]] usually comes after the subject.

When something else comes first, it is often for emphasis, a contrast, or a fresh start: [GEN 1:1] puts “in the beginning” before the verb: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים, word for word “in the beginning created God”. A Hebrew adjective follows its noun ([[adjective]]), and a sentence can have no verb at all ([[verbless-clause]]). Poetry moves words around much more freely.

entries.title: Verb stems: Qal, Piel, Hiphil and the rest
match: simple=the plain meaning of the root
intensive/resultive/transitive=a stronger, resulting or “making” sense
causative/declarative=causing someone to do it, or declaring it so
reflexive/iterative=doing it to oneself, or again and again
entries.short: A Hebrew root can be used in several patterns, called stems, that change the kind of action: simple, passive, intensive, causative or reflexive.

body.p: From one [[root]], Hebrew can make up to seven common verbs by fitting it into different patterns of vowels, prefixes and doubled letters. Each pattern is a stem (in Hebrew, *binyan*, “building”). Not every root is used in every stem, and the meanings are tendencies rather than rules: the dictionary gives each stem's meaning for each verb.

body.p: STEPBible's labels put a short description after each stem name, such as “Hiphil (causative/declarative, active)”. The descriptions say what the stem usually does: *simple*, *intensive/resultive/transitive* (a stronger action, or one that brings about a state; “transitive” means the verb takes an [[object]]), *causative/declarative* (making someone do something, or declaring something so), and *reflexive/iterative* (doing it to oneself, or repeatedly). The word “active” or “passive” after the description is the [[voice]]: whether the subject does the action or has it done to it. The app shows them as STEPBible writes them.
A few [[rare-stems]] are explained in their own entry, and the Aramaic stems in [[aramaic-stems]].

entries.title: Qal: the simple stem
match: qal=the simple stem
entries.short: The basic stem of a Hebrew verb, with its plain meaning: שָׁמַר, “he kept”. Most verbs in the Bible are Qal.

body.p: Qal means “light”, as in “simple”. It gives a root its plain meaning: אָמַר, “he said”, הָלַךְ, “he went”, שָׁמַר, “he kept”. Dictionaries list verbs by their Qal [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] form, “he did”, so the Qal is also the form you look up.
Its passive [[participle]] is labelled “Qal (simple, passive)”: בָּרוּךְ, “blessed”.

entries.title: Niphal
match: niphal=the passive or reflexive of the simple stem
entries.short: Usually the passive of the Qal: “he was kept”. Sometimes reflexive (“he hid himself”) or with a meaning of its own. It is marked by a נ at the front.

body.p: The Niphal adds נ before the root, which shows in the [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]]: נִשְׁמַר, “he was kept” or “he took care”. In other forms the נ merges into the next letter and leaves a doubling dot ([[dagesh]]): הִשָּׁמֶר, “be careful!”, literally “keep yourself”.
Most Niphal verbs are passive: נִקְרָא, “he was called”. Some are reflexive, “he hid himself”, and some simply have their own meaning, such as נִלְחַם, “he fought”.

entries.title: Piel
match: piel=the stem with a doubled middle letter: often “to make” or a stronger action
entries.short: A stem marked by a doubled middle letter of the root. It often means “to make something so” or a stronger, repeated action: קִדַּשׁ, “he made holy”.

body.p: The Piel doubles the middle letter of the root, shown by a [[dagesh]] in it: דִּבֶּר, with בּ. Older grammars called it the intensive stem. Scholars now describe it more as bringing about a state: from “to be holy”, Qal, comes “to make holy”, Piel. For many verbs it is just the usual stem: דִּבֶּר, “he spoke”, is Piel, and there is hardly any Qal of that verb.

entries.title: Pual
match: pual=the passive of the piel
entries.short: The passive of the [[piel]]: “it was made holy”. Like the Piel it doubles the middle letter, with a u-vowel at the start.

body.p: The Pual is not common. It has the Piel's doubled middle letter and a u-vowel (ֻ, called qibbuts) under the first: מְקֻדָּשׁ, “consecrated”. Many Pual forms in the Bible are [[participle|participles]].

entries.title: Hiphil
match: hiphil=the causative stem: “to make someone do”
entries.short: The causative stem: “to make someone do” the root's action. From “to come out” comes “to bring out”. It is marked by a ה at the front and often a י inside.

body.p: The Hiphil turns a verb of doing into a verb of causing: יָצָא, “he went out”, Qal; הוֹצִיא, “he brought out”, Hiphil. Its [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] starts with ה: הִשְׁמִיד, “he destroyed”. In other forms the ה is hidden after a prefix, but a long i-vowel, written with י, often shows before the last letter: יַשְׁמִיד, “he will destroy”.
Some Hiphil verbs declare rather than cause: הִצְדִּיקוּ, “they declare righteous”, from the root for “righteous”. That is why STEPBible's description says “causative/declarative”.

entries.title: Hophal
match: hophal=the passive of the hiphil
entries.short: The passive of the [[hiphil]]: “he was made to do”, “he was brought”. It is marked by an o or u vowel at the start.

body.p: The Hophal is rare. It is the [[hiphil]] turned passive: “he brought”, Hiphil; “he was brought”, Hophal. Its first syllable usually has a short o or u: הֻגַּד, “it was told”.

entries.title: Hithpael
match: hithpael=the reflexive stem: doing it to oneself
entries.short: The reflexive stem: doing the action to oneself or with each other, or going about doing it: הִתְקַדְּשׁוּ, “they sanctified themselves”, הִתְפַּלֵּל, “he prayed”.

body.p: The Hithpael adds הִתְ- at the front and doubles the middle letter like the [[piel]]. Its meaning is often reflexive (“to sanctify oneself”), sometimes doing something with one another, or repeatedly, or pretending: הִתְהַלֵּךְ, “he walked about”. הִתְפַּלֵּל, “he prayed”, is one of its commonest words.

When the root starts with ס, שׂ or שׁ, the ת swaps places with it: הִשְׁתַּמֵּר, “he kept himself”, not הִתְשַׁמֵּר. After צ the ת also becomes ט, and before ד, ט or ת it merges into a doubled letter.

entries.title: Rare stems
match: hishtaphel=a rare causative-reflexive stem, used for “bowing down”
tiphil=a rare causative stem with ת
nithpael=a rare passive of the hithpael
hothpaal=a rare passive of the hithpael
entries.short: A handful of verbs use stems outside the main seven. The best known is “to bow down” or “to worship”, הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה, labelled hishtaphel.

body.p: הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה, “he bowed down”, used for bowing to people and for worshipping God, is the commonest of these. Older grammars explained it as a reflexive form of a root שׁחה. Most now see it as the rare hishtaphel stem of the root חוה, and STEPBible labels it so.
The tiphil, nithpael and hothpaal appear only a few times each. When you meet one, the [[dictionary-form]] and the English in the verse are your guide.

Grammars also name patterns such as the polel and pilpel, in which a root with a weak middle letter repeats a letter to do the work of the [[piel]] (see [[weak-verbs]]). STEPBible counts these as Piel or [[hithpael|Hithpael]], so the app's labels don't use those names.

entries.title: Perfect (qatal)
match: perfect=the qatal form: an action seen as complete
entries.short: The Hebrew verb form with endings, qatal, usually for a completed action, which English mostly translates with the past: שָׁמַר, “he kept”.

body.p: The perfect is made by adding endings to the stem: שָׁמַר, “he kept”, שָׁמַרְתִּי, “I kept”, שָׁמְרוּ, “they kept”. Grammar books call it qatal, after the pattern קָטַל, “he killed”, the verb older grammars used as their model. They also call it the suffix conjugation (a conjugation is a set of verb forms), because the person is shown by a suffix.

It presents an action as complete. Usually that means the past, but not always: with verbs of state it can be present (יָדַעְתִּי, “I know”), and in promises and prophecy something so certain that it is spoken of as done. That is why STEPBible labels it “past/present”.
Joined to “and”, it often carries on a series of future or commanded actions: see [[weqatal]].

entries.title: Imperfect (yiqtol)
match: imperfect=the yiqtol form: an action seen as not complete
entries.short: The Hebrew verb form with prefixes, yiqtol, for actions not seen as complete: usually the future, but also habits, wishes and commands: יִשְׁמֹר, “he will keep”.

body.p: The imperfect adds a prefix that shows the person (א for “I”, ת for “you” and “she”, י for “he” and “they”, נ for “we”), and sometimes an ending too: יִשְׁמֹר, “he will keep”, תִּשְׁמְרוּ, “you will keep”. Grammar books call it yiqtol, or the prefix conjugation.

It presents an action as not complete. That can be the future (“he will keep”), something that happens again and again (“he used to keep”), something possible or wished (“he may keep”, “let him keep”), or a lasting command: לֹא תִּגְנֹב, “you shall not steal”. That range is why STEPBible's labels say “future/present” and sometimes add “indicative/jussive”.
Don't confuse it with the Greek [[imperfect-greek|imperfect]], which is a past [[tense]]. In stories, an imperfect with a special “and” in front is the main past form: see [[wayyiqtol]].

entries.title: Wayyiqtol: the narrative past
match: consecutive imperfect=the wayyiqtol: “and he did”, the narrative past
entries.short: “And” joined to an [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] form, used for the main events of a story in the past: וַיֹּאמֶר, “and he said”. It is the commonest verb form in Hebrew stories.

body.p: Biblical stories move forward with this form: וַיְהִי, “and it came to pass”, וַיֹּאמֶר, “and he said”, וַיֵּלֶךְ, “and he went”. It looks like an [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] with “and” in front, but it describes a completed past event, one after another in the story.

You can recognise it by the “and”: וַ, with a patah and a doubled letter after it (though a י with a [[shewa]] usually drops the doubling dot: וַיְהִי). Before א the vowel lengthens instead: וָאֹמַר, “and I said”. Its stress often moves towards the front of the word, which can shorten its last vowel.

STEPBible calls it the “consecutive imperfect”. The app's short label is “wayyiqtol”, the name most grammars now use. The name starts with w, as ו was probably said in the earliest times; the [[masoretes|Masoretes]], and the app, say v: va-YO-mer.

entries.title: Weqatal: “and he will”
match: consecutive perfect=the weqatal: “and he will”, carrying on a future or command
entries.short: “And” joined to a [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] form, used to carry on a series of future, habitual or commanded actions: וְאָמַרְתָּ, “and you shall say”.

body.p: Where the [[wayyiqtol]] carries a story forward in the past, the weqatal carries forward a series of actions that are future, repeated or commanded. After a command or a future verb, each following step is often a weqatal: “go, and you shall say to them…”.

It looks like a [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] with an ordinary וְ in front. Context shows the difference between it and a plain “and he did”. STEPBible calls it the “consecutive perfect”, and its labels mark the time “future/present”.

entries.title: Weyiqtol: “and” with an imperfect
match: conjunction+imperfect=an imperfect with an ordinary “and” in front (weyiqtol)
entries.short: An [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] with an ordinary “and” in front, often expressing purpose or a wish: “and let him go”, “so that he may go”.

body.p: This is not the narrative [[wayyiqtol]]: its “and” is the ordinary וְ, with no doubled letter after it. It often follows a command and gives its purpose, “do this, so that…”, or continues a wish. STEPBible labels it “conjunction+imperfect”.

entries.title: Jussive: “let him”
match: jussive=a wish or command for someone else: “let him”, “may it”
entries.short: A form of the [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] used to wish or command something of another person: יְהִי אוֹר, “let there be light”.

body.p: The jussive expresses the speaker's will for someone other than the one spoken to: “let him go”, “may the LORD bless you”. It looks like the [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]], and for most verbs it is exactly the same; for some it is a little shorter: יִהְיֶה, “it will be”, but יְהִי, “let it be”. With אַל in front it means “don't”: see [[prohibition]].
STEPBible's labels mark it “future/present jussive”, or “indicative/jussive” where the form could be either.

entries.title: Cohortative: “let me”, “let us”
match: cohortative=a wish or resolve for oneself: “let me”, “let us”
entries.short: A form of the [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] for the speaker's own wish or resolve: “let me go”, “let us go”, often with an extra ה at the end: נֵלְכָה, “let us go”.

body.p: The cohortative is the “I” and “we” partner of the [[imperative]] and [[jussive]]. It often has the [[paragogic|extra ending]] -ָה: אֵלְכָה, “let me go”, נֵלְכָה, “let us go”. Without that ending it may look just like an ordinary “I will” or “we will”, and only the context shows the wish.

entries.title: Infinitive construct
match: infinitive construct=the “to …” form of a Hebrew verb, also “when …”
entries.short: The Hebrew [[infinitive]] used like English “to …”, often with a preposition: לִשְׁמֹר, “to keep”; with בְּ or כְּ it means “when”: בְּבֹאוֹ, “when he came”.

body.p: The infinitive construct is the form most like an English [[infinitive]]. With לְ in front it means “to” or “in order to”: לֵאמֹר, literally “to say”, introduces speech like a colon, and English translates it “saying”. With בְּ or כְּ in front and a pronoun ending, it makes a time clause: “when he came”, “as they went”.

entries.title: Infinitive absolute
match: infinitive absolute=a form of the verb used to strengthen another verb: “surely”
entries.short: A form of the verb, often placed before another form of the same verb for emphasis: מוֹת תָּמוּת, “you will surely die”.

body.p: The infinitive absolute is an unusual [[infinitive]]: it doesn't change, takes no prefixes or endings, and is mostly used beside another verb from the same root, to make it stronger. מוֹת תָּמוּת, “dying you will die”, means “you will surely die” ([GEN 2:17]). English translates the effect with “surely”, “indeed” or “certainly”. It can also stand in for a command: זָכוֹר, “remember!”.

entries.title: Hebrew participles
match: participle=a verb used like an adjective or noun: “going”, “one who goes”
participle passive=a participle with a passive meaning: “kept”, “blessed”
entries.short: A verb used like an adjective or noun, for ongoing action or for someone who does something: שֹׁמֵר, “keeping”, “a keeper”; בָּרוּךְ, “blessed”.

body.p: The Hebrew [[participle]] often describes something going on at the time: הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי עֹמֵד, “look, I am standing”. As a noun it names someone by what they do: שֹׁמֵר, “a keeper”, רֹעֶה, “a shepherd”. It has the [[gender]] and [[number]] of an [[adjective]], not a [[person]], so “I am standing” and “he is standing” use the same word.
The Qal passive participle has a u-vowel: בָּרוּךְ, “blessed”, כָּתוּב, “written”. STEPBible labels it “participle passive”.

entries.title: “Past/present” and “future/present” in Hebrew labels
match: past/present indicative=a statement, usually about the past (or the present)
future/present indicative=a statement, usually about the future (or the present)
future/present jussive=a wish or command for someone else
future/present cohortative=a wish or resolve of the speaker
future/present indicative/jussive=a statement or a wish: the form can be either
future/present indicative/cohortative=a statement or a resolve: the form can be either
entries.short: STEPBible's Hebrew labels add a note in brackets on a verb's usual time and use. “Past/present” and “future/present” mean either may be right.

body.p: Hebrew verb forms don't fix time the way English tenses do: see [[aspect]]. So STEPBible's labels add a reminder in brackets. “Past/present indicative” after a [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] or [[wayyiqtol]] means a statement, usually about the past. “Future/present indicative” after an [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]] or [[weqatal]] means a statement, usually about the future.
Where the form could be a statement or a wish, the label says so: “indicative/jussive” or “indicative/cohortative”. In each case, the English in the verse shows how the translators read it.

entries.title: Person, gender and number: 3ms, 2fp and the like
entries.short: Under Hebrew words the app shortens person, gender and number to three characters: 3ms means “he” (3rd person, masculine, singular); 1cp means “we”.

body.p: The digit is the [[person]]: 1 “I/we”, 2 “you”, 3 “he/she/they”. The first letter is the [[gender]]: m masculine, f feminine, c common (either). The last is the [[number]]: s singular, p plural, d [[dual]]. So:
Nouns and participles have no person, so they show only gender and number: ms, fp. The same letters appear on [[pronoun-suffix|pronoun endings]]: “suffix 3ms” is “his” or “him”.

entries.title: Weak verbs: roots with a missing or changing letter
entries.short: Roots that contain א, ה, ו, י or נ, or a throat letter, often lose or change a letter: נָתַן, “he gave”, becomes יִתֵּן, “he will give”, without its first נ.

body.p: Regular verbs keep all three root letters in every form. Many common verbs don't. A נ at the start often vanishes and leaves a doubled letter ([[dagesh]]): יִתֵּן from נתן. A ה at the end often disappears or becomes another vowel: בָּנָה, “he built”, וַיִּבֶן, “and he built”. A ו or י in the middle can turn into a vowel: קוּם, “to rise”, קָם, “he rose”. [[gutturals|Throat letters]] change the vowels around them.
Grammars name these verbs by the position of the weak letter: I-nun means a נ first (נתן), III-he a ה last (בנה), and a hollow verb has ו or י in the middle (קום).
When a word seems to have only two root letters, it is probably one of these. The app always shows the [[dictionary-form]], so you can see the full root.

entries.title: Aramaic verb stems
entries.short: Aramaic verbs use [[stems]] like Hebrew ones, with different names: the [[peal]] is the plain one, the [[pael]] doubles a letter, and the [[haphel|Haphel]] means “make someone do”.

body.p: Aramaic builds its verbs the same way as Hebrew: a [[root]] fitted into a pattern called a stem. The patterns match closely, but grammars use Aramaic names for them. Both sets of names are made by fitting the model verb פעל, “to do”, into each pattern: the Hebrew [[piel|Piel]] and the Aramaic Pael are that verb in the doubling pattern of each language.

body.p: Aramaic verb forms are the [[perfect-hebrew|perfect]] and [[imperfect-hebrew|imperfect]], as in Hebrew, but without the narrative “and” forms ([[wayyiqtol]] and [[weqatal]]). Stories in Aramaic usually use the perfect, or a [[participle]], for the past.

entries.title: Peal
match: peal=the simple stem of Aramaic, like the Hebrew Qal
entries.short: The simple stem of Aramaic verbs, matching the Hebrew [[qal]]: אֲמַר, “he said”.

body.p: Most Aramaic verbs in Daniel and Ezra are Peal. It gives the root its plain meaning, active: אֲמַר, “he said”, עֲנוֹ, “they answered”. The common Aramaic phrase עָנֵה… וְאָמַר, “answering… and saying”, is Peal.

entries.title: Peil
match: peil=the passive of the simple stem in Aramaic
entries.short: The passive of the [[peal]], used a few times in Daniel and Ezra: “it was written”, “it was given”.

body.p: The Peil turns the simple stem [[passive]]: יְהִיבַת, “it was given”. It is rare, and a passive meaning is the clue.

entries.title: Pael
match: pael=the stem with a doubled middle letter, like the Hebrew Piel
entries.short: The Aramaic stem with a doubled middle letter, matching the Hebrew [[piel]]: מְשַׁבַּח, “praising”.

body.p: Like the Piel, the Pael doubles the middle letter of the root with a [[dagesh]], and often has a “making” or stronger meaning. Some verbs simply use it as their usual stem: מְשַׁבַּח, “praising”, in [DAN 2:23|Daniel 2:23].

entries.title: Haphel, aphel and shaphel
match: haphel=the causative stem of Aramaic, like the Hebrew Hiphil
aphel=the causative stem of Aramaic, with א instead of ה
shaphel=a rare causative stem with שׁ
ishtaphel=a rare reflexive of the shaphel
entries.short: The causative stems of Aramaic: “to make someone do”. The Haphel starts with ה, the Aphel with א, and the rare Shaphel with שׁ.

body.p: These match the Hebrew [[hiphil]]: הַשְׁפֵּלְתְּ, “you have humbled” ([DAN 5:22]), is Haphel. The Aphel is the same stem with א in place of the ה, a later spelling. The Shaphel starts with שׁ and is used by a few verbs, especially שֵׁיזִב, “he rescued”. The ishtaphel is a rare reflexive form of it.
Their passive is the [[hophal]], which STEPBible labels with the Hebrew name.

entries.title: Hitpeel and hitpaal
match: hitpeel=the passive or reflexive of the Peal
hitpaal=the passive or reflexive of the Pael
hitpael=the passive or reflexive of the Pael
entries.short: The Aramaic stems that start with הִתְ- and are passive or reflexive: the Hitpeel of the [[peal]], and the Hitpaal of the [[pael]].

body.p: Aramaic has no [[niphal]]. For “to be done”, it puts הִתְ- or אִתְ- in front of the simple or the doubled stem: תִּתְבְּנֵא, “it will be built”, in the letters in Ezra. STEPBible's labels spell these stems in more than one way (hitpeel, hitpaal, hitpael); all of them are passive or reflexive.

entries.title: “The” in Aramaic: the definite ending
match: definite=with “the”: the ending -א
entries.short: Aramaic says “the” with an ending, usually -א: מַלְכָּא, “the king”, from מֶלֶךְ, “a king”. STEPBible's labels call this form “definite”.

body.p: Hebrew puts “the” at the front of a word ([[hebrew-article]]). Aramaic puts it at the end: מֶלֶךְ is “a king”, מַלְכָּא is “the king”. Grammars call this the emphatic or determined state. Besides this form, Aramaic nouns have the [[absolute-state|absolute]] and [[construct-state|construct]] forms, just as Hebrew ones do.
The ending also shows in Aramaic words the New Testament keeps, such as Αββα, “Father”, from אַבָּא.

entries.title: What a tapped word shows
entries.short: Tap any Greek or Hebrew word in the Reader to see the word as it stands, its English in this verse, its [[dictionary-form]] and meaning, its grammar and how common it is.

body.p: The details open in a panel from the bottom of the screen. From the top:

ul: the word as written, with its [[transliteration]] and a Listen button;
**In this verse**: the English for this word here, from STEPBible's word-by-word translation ([[gloss]]);
**Word parts** (Hebrew): each [[prefixes|prefix]], the main word and any [[pronoun-suffix|ending]], with their meanings;
**Dictionary form**: the form you would look up ([[dictionary-form]]), with its [[strongs|Strong's number]];
**Dictionary meaning**: the word's usual meaning;
**Grammar**: its grammar label, a plain description, and the link “What do these words mean?”, which explains each part of the label;
**How common**: how often the dictionary form appears ([[how-common]]).

body.p: Below, the verse's English shows for context, and Previous and Next move along the verse. Tapping the dictionary form opens the full entry in the [[words-tab|Words tab]]. Today's verse and a lesson's Read step show a shorter version of the same details.

entries.short: With Grammar switched on in the Reader's display options, each word has a short label under it. This is every short form used there, and what it stands for.
